- held none of the player's text in either surface;
- warned only about the failed requests: the three warnings that named the
  player were gone, and so were the withheld accessibility snapshot (a frame
  had detached) and the scroll positions not put back.

Two recognized blocks remain lower down: the author's photo read as "aot"
at 19 %, and a 44-pixel social icon read as "in". Both were in the first
capture too, and they are P23-6's case, which is still not changed.

`tests/test_ad_units.py` captures `tests/fixtures/ad_player_page.html`. The
fixture holds the player's markup, an AdSense unit and a Publisher Tag slot,
beside article content named like an ad: an "Advertisement" picture, a
`download-header`, an `mv-notes` section. The ad text must be absent from
`content.md` and the PDF in clean mode and present in faithful mode, and the
article's text must stay in order. The clean-mode test fails on master.

## P78: a bot check's page served with 200, and an HTTP/2 reset (2026-10-17)

A week after P23, the same kind of capture (every page one course module
linked to) met two more refusals of an automated browser that WebShot did not
name. Master was d247610.


### P78-1: a bot check's page was captured as the page, exit 0

A business magazine's article, captured in faithful mode, exited 0 with a
7-page PDF whose text was a block page under the article's title: "We
detected unusual activity from your device or network", a list of reasons
(rapid taps or clicks, automated use, developer tools) and an ID. No warning.
P23-3 names a bot check only from a 403's headers, and this answer was a 200.
The same site is the one P23-3 measured answering 403 with `server:
DataDome`.

Read again on 2026-10-17, the article was served whole, with 200 and
`x-datadome: protected` on the response. That header is on the site's
ordinary answer, which confirms P23-3's choice not to treat it as evidence of
a refusal. The block page's wording is DataDome's own: people refused by
other sites behind DataDome quote it word for word, and DataDome serves its
challenge and block pages from `geo.captcha-delivery.com`, in a frame its tag
draws over the page it refuses. The frame itself was not seen in this
capture: its PDF had been replaced by a capture of a copy saved from Chrome
before the cause was looked for.

The page is now read after the lazy-load pass (`bot_check_page`), for three
signatures, each the vendor naming itself:

| Vendor | Signature | Why only that |
|---|---|---|
| DataDome | an `iframe` whose `src` host is `captcha-delivery.com` or under it, laid out and shown | a frame laid out invisibly blocks nothing |
| HUMAN (formerly PerimeterX) | a rendered `#px-captcha` | the element is sized by a frame its script loads, so a box of any size counts |
| Akamai | the title "Access Denied" **and** a `Reference #` in Akamai's dotted format | the title alone is an ordinary phrase, and an article about Akamai could quote a reference |

Each fails the capture with exit 4, the bot check named, "this is not a
sign-in page", and P23-3's advice to save the page from one's own browser.
The QA report records the status (200) and `final_url`, as P23-3 made it do
for a refused status. P22's rule stands: no phrase of a block page is
matched, so an article that quotes one, links to the vendor's host or names
the element is captured. The test runs on the top document and every open
shadow root, and not on a local file, which is what the person saved.

It runs after the lazy-load pass because a check that watches for rapid
scrolling can draw its page during that pass, and before anything is
extracted, because nothing of a bot check's page is the page. A page that
cannot be read is read once more after the document loads, as the sign-in
check does (P22-1). A second failure is a manifest warning that the test did
not run, never a pass.

### P78-2: Akamai and HUMAN were matched from their documented pages

Neither was met in this capture. HUMAN's block page is titled "Access to this
page has been denied" and holds `<div id="px-captcha">`, where its script
draws the press-and-hold button. Akamai's refusal reads "You don't have
permission to access … on this server" under the title "Access Denied", with
a reference such as `Reference #18.6f1d2c17.1792000000.1a2b3c4d` and the same
number on an `errors.edgesuite.net` link. P23-3 left Akamai out because no
page had shown it; it is in now because the module's issue list asked for it,
and the two-part signature keeps it from matching an article.

### P78-3: `ERR_HTTP2_PROTOCOL_ERROR` read as a site that is down

A news site's article failed with exit 3 and "could not be reached:
Page.goto: net::ERR_HTTP2_PROTOCOL_ERROR". The same page opened in Chrome a
minute later. Resetting the stream at the HTTP/2 layer is how Akamai's bot
manager is commonly reported to refuse a headless browser, and the message
sent the reader to the site. The message now adds that the server broke off
the connection at the HTTP/2 layer, which is how some bot checks refuse an
automated browser, and the same advice (`http2_refusal_hint`). It is a "may",
because a server or proxy with a broken HTTP/2 stack raises the same code,
and the exit code stays 3: nothing in the answer names a bot check.

`ERR_HTTP2_PING_FAILED` was suggested with it and is not matched. Chromium
raises it when the server stops answering its HTTP/2 pings, which is a
connection that went quiet, the usual sign of a network that dropped. Telling
that reader to save the page by hand would send them the wrong way, as P23-3's
sign-in advice did.

### P78-4: the tests

`tests/test_bot_check_pages.py` serves each vendor's page from a loopback
server with 200, and answers DataDome's host from a route inside the browser,
so nothing leaves the machine. Each of the three signatures fails with exit 4,
the vendor named, the advice, `http_status` 200 and `final_url`, and no PDF.
So does a DataDome frame that the page adds only when it is first scrolled.
An article that quotes the block page, links to the vendor's host, names the
element and carries an Akamai reference under another title is captured, and
so is a page whose frame and `#px-captcha` are present and not shown. A page
whose every read fails reports that the test did not run. The HTTP/2 message
is tested from `goto` raising Chromium's error, because Chromium speaks HTTP/2
only over TLS to a certificate it trusts, which a loopback server is not. On
master the four refusals and the frame test exit 0, and the HTTP/2 message
lacks the advice.

### P78-5: what this does not cover

- A site's own block page that names no vendor. Matching its words is the
  thing P22 declined.
- A check that draws its page after the lazy-load pass, while the bundle is
  being built.
- Akamai's page served as a 403, which still gets P23-3's two readings: the
  403 path reads the response headers, and Akamai's name no check.

## P79: a consent dialog printed over the article, in both modes (2026-10-17)

From the capture that produced P78. Master was d247610.


### P79-1: what was printed

An international forum's article was captured in faithful mode, and its
Cookiebot dialog ("This website uses cookies…", three buttons) was printed
on top of the last two paragraphs. The text layer interleaved the two: "we
need the security foundation that"marketing" will makecookies it
trustworthy". No warning. `--exclude "#CybotCookiebotDialog"` fixed it.

Captured again on 2026-10-17 in clean mode, the default, the result was worse
than the issue said. The dialog was on five of the six pages, because it is
fixed to the window and Chromium prints a fixed box on every page, and its
text was in `content.md` and `content.txt`. The interleaved sentence was the
same, word for word. Clean mode has two rules that might have caught it and
neither did. The noise list's cookie selectors look for `cookie` in an
`aria-label` or `cookie-consent` in a class or id, and the dialog's root is
`<div id="CybotCookiebotDialog" role="region">`. And the large-overlay rule
wants a fixed box at least 45 % of the window wide, which a corner dialog is
not.

### P79-2: both modes hide the consent managers by name

`CONSENT_MANAGERS` lists seven vendors by the ids and classes their scripts
give their own dialogs:

| Vendor | Selectors |
|---|---|
| Cookiebot | `#CybotCookiebotDialog`, `#CybotCookiebotDialogBodyUnderlay` |
| OneTrust | `#onetrust-consent-sdk` |
| Didomi | `#didomi-host` |
| Quantcast Choice | `.qc-cmp2-container` |
| TrustArc | `#truste-consent-track` |
| Usercentrics | `#usercentrics-root`, `#usercentrics-cmp-ui` |
| Sourcepoint | `[id^='sp_message_container']` |

Cookiebot's dialog was measured on this page. The others follow each vendor's
documented markup and were not met in a capture, the standard P23-9 set for
the ad units. Every selector is a name the vendor gave its own element, so
none can match a page's own box the way `[class*='cookie-consent' i]` can.
That is why these are hidden in faithful mode too, and the noise list is
not.

Faithful mode used to hide nothing (docs/04 §5 item 5). It hides these now,
because a consent dialog is not the page. It is the browser's session being
asked a question that a person would have answered before reading, it covers
the page's text on every printed page, and its words land in the bundle in
the middle of the page's sentences. A faithful capture that keeps it records
the page less accurately, not more. A manifest warning names each vendor
whose dialog was on screen, with the selector that found it. A manager whose
container is on every page and whose banner was already closed is hidden as
well, and is not named, because hiding it changed nothing a reader would see.
"On screen" counts the container and everything inside it, including an open
shadow root, since Usercentrics draws its banner inside one on a host with
no box of its own.

Recaptured live with the change, in both modes, the page had six pages, no
dialog text in the PDF or `content.md`, the sentence whole ("the security
foundation that will make it trustworthy"), and the warning naming Cookiebot.

The spec's item 5 also said clean mode "records the hidden-element count in
the manifest". No producer ever did: the count is logged ("Removed N
non-document element(s)"). The spec now says it is logged.

### P79-3: the tests

`tests/test_consent_dialogs.py` captures `tests/fixtures/consent_dialog_page.html`
in both modes. The fixture has a Cookiebot-shaped corner dialog, a closed
OneTrust banner, and a Usercentrics banner in a shadow root, beside article
text that names the vendors and has a box classed `cookie-notes`. The
dialogs' text must be absent from every PDF page and from `content.md`, the
article's text present, and the manifest's one consent warning must name
Cookiebot and Usercentrics and not OneTrust. Both modes fail on master.

### P79-4: what this does not cover

- A consent dialog from a vendor not on the list, or a site's own. The issue
  also suggested a warning for any fixed box that covers the page's text in
  the printed layout. It is not built here. The golden corpus's main fixture
  has a fixed cookie banner of its own over its text, which faithful mode
  keeps on purpose, so the warning would change every faithful golden of that
  page. And Chromium prints a fixed box on every page, so overlap has to be
  measured on the paginated layout, not on the screen. P83 builds it, and
  measures that the fixture's banner covers no printed text.
- A consent manager inside a frame, other than through the container that
  holds the frame (Sourcepoint's).
- The scroll lock a dialog leaves on `html` or `body` once it is hidden.
  None was seen to change what printed.

## P83: a fixed or sticky box printed over the page's text, now named (2026-10-17)

P79-4 left out the general warning: a fixed box that covers the page's text
in the printed layout. This builds it. The branch starts from #245, which adds
P79; master was fe97b28. Measured with Chromium 153.0.8010.12 (Playwright
1.63.0) and pypdfium2 5.13.0 (PDFium 153.0.7999.0), at WebShot's default page
box: Letter, 0.6in margins, scale 0.9, which lays out 779 × 1045 CSS px a page.

### P83-1: how Chromium prints fixed and sticky boxes

A test page of 60 short paragraphs and seven positioned boxes was printed with
Playwright at a 1280 × 900 window and read back object by object with PDFium:

| Box | What the five-page PDF held |
|---|---|
| fixed header, `top: 0`, 50px, `z-index: 10` | drawn on every page at the same place, after the page's own text, over the first lines of pages 2 to 5 |
| paragraph, `position: relative; z-index: 20` | drawn after the header |
| fixed box in a corner | drawn on every page |
| fixed full-window layer, no background, `pointer-events: none` | only its child's text drawn |
| fixed box, `opacity: 0` | not drawn at all |
| fixed box, `opacity: 0.7` | drawn inside a form XObject with fill alpha 179/255 |
| sticky, `top: 0` | drawn where it sits in the flow |
| sticky, `bottom: 0`, last in the document | drawn on page 1, 930 to 962px down the page's layout, over the last line of a paragraph, not where it sits at the document's end |

The sticky bar's place moves with the window. At WebShot's 1000px window it
was drawn across the break between pages 1 and 2, over the first line of page
2.

Two more boxes settled how a box can be measured. Every CSS filter function,
even one that changes nothing (`opacity(1)`, `brightness(1)`, `blur(0px)`),
printed the box as a picture, with no text left in it. `filter:
url(#missing)`, a reference to no filter, and `backdrop-filter` printed it as
vectors.

P79-4 also said the golden corpus's main fixture has a fixed cookie banner
over its text. On screen it does. Printed, the bar is on all three pages of
`article-faithful`, 43.9 to 85.7pt above each page's bottom edge, and every
page's text ends above it, so it covers none and no golden moves (P83-6).

### P83-2: what the warning measures

After the render, and before the clipping check, whose narrower viewport can
load images and move the layout, `render/covering.py` finds every outermost
element whose computed `position` is `fixed` or `sticky` and which has a box,
in the document and its open shadow roots. What the capture hid (P79's consent
managers, clean mode's noise, `--exclude`) is `display: none`, has no box, and
is not a candidate.

Each box is then painted in a colour of its own: its text, backgrounds,
borders, outlines, SVG fills and pseudo-elements, at the alpha each colour
had, in a colour the page does not use. A picture or a background picture in
the box paints its whole box in the colour, because its pixels carry none of
the box's. Shadows are switched off, and a filter is swapped for
`url(#webshot-ink-no-filter)`, which prints the box as vectors and, as any
filter does, keeps it the containing block of its fixed descendants, where
`filter: none` would move them. The page's own pictures are hidden, which
paints nothing new and moves nothing.

The page is printed a second time with the render's page box and backgrounds,
untagged, and PDFium reads every page: each object in paint order, its bounds
carried out of any form XObject and cut to its clip, its alpha times its
groups'; and each character, with its box and the object that drew it. A
character of the page's text is covered when one of the box's objects is
drawn later, at least half opaque, over the character's centre. Paint order is
z-order, so text the page raises above the box is not covered. Alpha is
opacity. `pointer-events` is never read, because nothing about it prints.

Not counted: spaces; characters drawn at under half opacity, such as the
recognized-text layer at 1% (P16-20); and text a fixed box draws, its own or
another fixed box's, because chrome over chrome is the same on screen as in
print. A sticky box's text is in the page's flow and is counted.

One warning per box that covers anything names it as a selector (tag, id, up
to three classes, and its parent when it has no id), the pages where it
covers text, the characters and the distinct lines covered, the first covered
stretch up to 60 characters, and the `--exclude` that leaves it out:

> A fixed box, div.notice-bar, prints over 50 characters of the page's text in
> 2 lines on both pages, starting "Under the notice bar, line one". The text
> stays in the PDF's text layer, but on the page the box is drawn over it.
> Pass --exclude "div.notice-bar" to capture the page without the box.

What would make the count wrong is a warning of its own. A box whose colours
did not take, because a page's inline `!important` outranks any sheet, is
named with what it kept. A marking that moved any element's layout, a
measuring print that failed or whose page count differs from the PDF's, and
text in it whose characters PDFium tied to no object, so that none could be
covered, each mean no measurement, and the warning says which.

### P83-3: a box on every page

A box Chromium repeats on every page is named once, never per page. The
warning names the pages where it covers text, because those are what a reader
loses, and also the pages it prints on when there are more. A pinned header
over the blank top of page 1 and over the first lines of every later page
reads:

> A fixed box, div > div.fixed.inset-x-0.top-0, prints on all 9 pages, and
> over 423 characters of the page's text in 18 lines on pages 2-9, ...

There is no minimum. A corner widget over the last three letters of one line
is reported as three characters, and the count tells the reader how much it
matters. A box over blank margin only, like the main fixture's bar, is not
reported at all.

Measured on 14 public pages in both modes, captured live with `--no-ocr`.
Each warning marked † was checked against a rendering of the page it names.


| # | Page | Mode | Pages | Boxes | Measured in | Warning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | an international forum's article (P79's) | faithful | 6 | 2 | 0.20s | fixed navigation placeholder: 95 characters, 4 lines, pages 2-3 and 6 † |
| | | clean | 6 | 8 | 0.24s | fixed navigation bar: 57 characters, 2 lines, pages 2-3 |
| 2 | a web reference's article | both | 16, 15 | 0 | | none |
| 3 | an encyclopedia article | both | 5 | 1 | 0.18s | none |
| 4 | a language's library reference | faithful | 23 | 1 | 0.86s | none |
| | | clean | 23 | 0 | | none |
| 5 | a WordPress blog's index | both | 7 | 1 | 0.21s | none (P83-4) |
| 6 | a technology news site's index | faithful | 26 | 2 | 1.44s | fixed privacy banner, printed on all 26 pages: 1,549 characters, 44 lines, on 10 of them † |
| | | clean | 22 | 1 | 0.45s | none: clean mode left the banner out |
| 7 | a broadcaster's technology index | faithful | 11 | 5 | 0.32s | sticky subscription bar: 224 characters, 6 lines, page 1 † |
| | | clean | 10 | 3 | 0.27s | sticky subscription bar: 152 characters, 3 lines, page 1 |
| 8 | a technology magazine's front page | faithful | 13 | 6 | 0.52s | fixed advertising frame: 27 characters, 2 lines, page 1 † |
| | | clean | 12 | 5 | 0.36s | none |
| 9 | a newspaper's technology index | faithful | 5 | 1 | 0.17s | none |
| | | clean | 5 | 0 | | none |
| 10 | a CSS specification | both | 44, 42 | 0 | | none |
| 11 | a CSS framework's documentation | both | 9 | 6 | 0.41s, 0.36s | fixed header, printed on all 9 pages: 423 characters, 18 lines, pages 2-9 † |
| 12 | a UI library's tutorial | both | 18 | 12 | 1.39s, 1.51s | none |
| 13 | a cloud provider's documentation | both | 6 | 0 | | none |
| 14 | a code host's documentation | both | 4 | 4 | 0.17s | none |

Five of the fourteen pages printed a box over their text in at least one
mode, and three of the five in clean mode, the default. The rendered pages
showed what each † warning claims: the forum's logo on an off-white band over
the heading "Have you read?" at the top of page 2; the privacy banner over a
headline at the bottom of page 2; the subscription bar halfway down page 1
over a lead headline; a video advertisement over all of page 1 under the
magazine's header, which the page draws above it and the warning does not
count; and the framework's header over the top of page 3, one of the eight
pages it names.

Sites change between loads. A second faithful capture of the news site the
same afternoon found the banner over 1,782 characters in 50 lines, on 12 of
25 pages.

### P83-4: an inline colour moved a box on a WordPress blog

The first version wrote the colours into each element's `style` attribute,
with `!important`, which no page rule outranks. On the WordPress blog
(page 5), clean mode then warned that a sticky box covered 48 characters, "Copilot SDK
for Java", on page 3. The PDF published beside it shows the line in full.

The box, `div#ghcc`, is empty: `position: sticky; bottom: 0; z-index: 99999`
and 0px tall. In the measuring print it was 6px tall, drawn across the page
over that line. The blog's block styles hold, for each side,
`html :where([style^="border-top-color"], [style*=";border-top-color"],
[style*="; border-top-color"]) { border-top-style: solid; }`, so that a block
given a border colour in the editor shows its border. Setting
`border-top-color` inline gave the box a solid `medium` border, 3px, top and
bottom: the colours had changed the layout they were measuring.

The colours now come from an adopted stylesheet whose rules match an attribute
on each painted element, at a specificity (eight ids, through `:is()`) no page
rule reaches, and nothing writes a `style` attribute. Elements with the same
declarations share a rule, so a box of thousands of elements adds a handful.
The cost is that a page's own inline `!important` colour now beats the
marking, and that box is reported as not marked. Before printing, the layout
of every element (`offsetLeft`, `offsetTop`, `offsetWidth`, `offsetHeight`) is
compared with what it was before marking, after a frame in which the page's
own scripts could react. Given one inline `border-top-color` on an empty
sticky box under those rules, the comparison reports 4 elements moved, the
first `html from 0,0,1280,76 to 0,0,1280,87`. The blog's warning is gone in
both modes.

### P83-5: the measuring print's cost

The first measuring print printed the page's pictures too. On the
broadcaster's page in clean mode that took 5.63s for 11 pages, the PDF
published beside it being 37.6 MB. With the page's pictures hidden it took
0.21s and 0.27s on two later captures of the same page, and 0.17s to 1.51s
across the table above. A page with no fixed or sticky box pays one script
run and no print.

### P83-6: the tests

`tests/fixtures/covering_boxes_page.html` lays out two pages of 30px lines
that never wrap, so every line sits at the same place in any font. It holds a
fixed notice bar over one line on each page and, on page 2, a line the page
raises above the bar; a sticky masthead; a fixed badge in the gutter; a fixed
panel at 30% opacity over text; a fixed full-window layer with
`pointer-events: none`; and a Cookiebot dialog over text. In both modes the
manifest's warnings, P79's aside, are exactly one: the notice bar, 50
characters in 2 lines on both pages. With `--exclude "div.notice-bar"` there
is none.

`tests/test_covered_text.py` also holds the rule on PDFium's records directly
(paint order, alpha, a character's centre, chrome over chrome, a box that was
not marked, the sample, the pages), the warnings' wording, and a browser test
that marks and restores a page holding the blog's border rules, a
pseudo-element, an inline `!important` colour, a shadow root with a transition
and an SVG: the colours take where they can, no element moves, the inline
colour is reported, and the page's markup, colours and adopted sheets come
back as they were.

No golden moved: the only golden page with a fixed box is the main fixture,
whose bar covers no text (P83-1).

### P83-7: what this does not cover

- A fixed box inside a frame, which prints inside the frame's box. A frame's
  text under a box of the page's is counted.
- A picture: one in a box counts as covering its whole box, transparent parts
  too, and the page's pictures under a box are not counted, only its text.
- A box's shadow, which is drawn over the text below a pinned header but
  rarely hides it.
- A page script that reacts to the marking without moving anything, such as
  one that repaints a box, between the layout check and the print.
- Text Chromium prints smaller than 0.25px, whose narrow letters PDFium does
  not read (P20-8). The recognized-text layer is the only such text WebShot
  prints, and it is not counted anyway.
- Moving or hiding any of these boxes. Which is chrome and which is the page
  is the reader's call, and `--exclude` is the remedy the warning names.
## P84 — dependency updates that stopped without a word (2026-10-17)

A review on 2026-10-17 found that dependency updates had stopped arriving for
about a week, and nothing had said so. What webshot-ai's record showed that
day:

- Dependabot opened nine pull requests on 2026-10-13, webshot-ai#25 to #33.
  Five were uv bumps, which is the limit of five open pull requests per
  ecosystem. None ran CI for days, because every workflow had been turned off.
  With five uv bumps open, Dependabot proposed no other uv update. Markdown
  3.11, released on 2026-09-25, was never proposed, and docling-slim was eight
  releases behind (2.132.0 against 2.140.0).
- webshot-ai#26 and #28 passed every check and stayed open, because GitHub had
  turned their auto-merge off (P84-3).
- The one check that looked for stale bumps read an empty answer as "none
  stale".

No part of the pipeline failed in a way that sends an email. Dependabot has
nothing to report when it reaches its limit, a pull request that never runs
CI never fails, and a disabled workflow is silent.

### P84-1 — judging the pipeline by its results: the dependency watch

`tools/audit/staleness.py`, run daily by `.github/workflows/dependency-watch.yml`
on a GitHub-hosted runner, asks whether updates are arriving, not whether each
part of the pipeline is running. It judges three things:

- **Direct dependencies.** Every package `pyproject.toml` names, at the
  version `uv.lock` pins, against PyPI. A pin is stale once the *first*
  release newer than it has been out longer than Dependabot's cooldown for
  that kind of release (P84-2) plus 14 days. That allows one weekly run to
  propose the release and one more week to merge it. The wait counts from the
  first newer release, not the newest: a project that releases every week
  always has a fresh newest release, so measuring from that would never find
  the lock behind. Pre-releases, and releases whose files are all yanked, do
  not count, and a pinned version that PyPI has yanked or does not list is a
  finding of its own.
- **Pinned actions.** Every `uses: owner/repo@<sha> # <tag>` in the workflows
  is judged against the action's releases by the same rule. The tag in the
  comment must also still name the pinned commit. In March 2025 every tag of
  tj-actions/changed-files was moved to a malicious commit. A SHA pin is safe
  from that, but the next bump, made from the tag, is not. A `uses:` with no
  SHA, or with no tag comment, is a finding.
- **Dependabot's pull requests.** Four cases are findings: a bump whose checks
  failed (at once), a bump older than 6 h that no check has run on, a bump
  older than 6 h whose auto-merge is off, and a bump open for 72 h. Each finding
  names its remedy.

Transitive pins are not judged. Dependabot proposes direct dependencies only,
and a transitive pin moves when what depends on it allows it to. On
2026-10-17, 64 of the 148 transitive pins were behind PyPI. The oldest was
antlr4-python3-runtime 4.9.3, 1,650 days behind. An alarm that is always red
is one nobody reads. tools/audit/check.py audits the transitive pins for
vulnerabilities, and the watch prints how many pins it left unjudged.

An update can be held back on purpose in `tools/audit/holds.toml`, with a
reason and a date to look again. An expired hold is a finding, and so is a
hold on something no longer behind, so the list cannot outlive its reasons.

The watch fails loudly when it cannot judge. A lock that pins nothing, a
direct dependency the lock does not pin, a PyPI or GitHub answer that does
not come, a malformed hold, or a crash makes the run INCOMPLETE (exit 2),
which fails it as surely as a stale pin does (exit 1). It keeps one issue
open, "dependencies: updates have stalled". The body is rewritten on every
run, and a comment is added only when a problem appears that the issue did
not already list, so each notification means something new. The issue is
written with the workflow's token, so it is GitHub Actions' and GitHub
notifies the owner of it. An issue written with the owner's own token
notifies nobody. The issue also mentions the owner. If the check dies before
it reaches the issue, the workflow's last step opens one anyway. The issues
are listed, never searched: a search once answered another repository's
token with nothing.

Run on 2026-10-17 against webshot-ai's master (2b10d2d) with that day's PyPI
and pull requests, it found 3 problems in 28 direct pins, 10 pinned actions
and 1 open Dependabot pull request:
- markdown 3.10.3, 22 days behind 3.11 (minor; 21 days allowed);
- webshot-ai#30 (trafilatura 2.3.1), whose golden corpus had failed;
- the same bump, open 110 h.

A scheduled run that day would have opened the issue with those three.

`tests/test_dependency_staleness.py` holds each threshold at its edge, the
first-newer rule, yanked and missing versions, holds and their expiry, the
`uses:` parsing (commented lines are not read), a moved tag, every pull
request case, and each input that cannot be read. It also holds the
listing's freedom from search, the issue's open, rewrite, comment and close,
a crash that still reaches the issue, the cooldown against `dependabot.yml`,
and the workflow's shape.

### P84-2 — a release on its first day: the cooldown

A green bump merges itself, so a release proposed on its first day is
installed on its first day. The first days are when a hijacked, broken or
withdrawn release is still live. Compromised releases of ultralytics on PyPI
(December 2024) and the moved tags of tj-actions/changed-files (March 2025)
were each found and pulled within about a day. `dependabot.yml` had no
`cooldown`, which GitHub's options reference says leaves version updates at
a default of three days.

Each ecosystem now names its own cooldown:

| Ecosystem | Patch | Minor | Major | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| uv | 3 days | 7 days | 14 days | 7 days |
| GitHub Actions | 7 days | 7 days | 7 days | 7 days |

The reasons for each:

- **uv, patch.** Patch releases are fixes and should arrive soon, and three
  days outlasts the incidents above.
- **uv, minor.** A minor release adds features and, with them, regressions,
  which a week usually brings out.
- **uv, major.** A major release breaks an API on purpose. It usually needs a
  bridge change and re-recorded goldens anyway, and its first fixes follow
  within two weeks, so waiting for them costs nothing.
- **GitHub Actions.** Dependabot accepts only `default-days` for actions; the
  options reference lists GitHub Actions among the ecosystems the semver keys
  do not support. An action runs with the job's token, and its tags are what
  an attacker moves, so a week. An action bump is rarely urgent.

Security updates are not delayed by any of this. GitHub's reference says
cooldown is only for version updates, and Dependabot sends a security update
as soon as its advisory exists.

The watch's thresholds are these numbers plus 14 days. `COOLDOWN_DAYS` in
staleness.py and `dependabot.yml` are held to each other by
`test_the_alarm_and_dependabot_agree_on_the_cooldown`, so the alarm cannot
expect a release earlier than the pipeline will propose it.

### P84-3 — a bump that edits a workflow, behind a base whose workflows moved

webshot-ai#26 (setup-uv 10.3.0) and #28 (upload-artifact 7.0.2) both edit
`ci.yml` and `release.yml`. After they were opened, #27 changed
`release.yml` on master, at 2026-10-17 16:54Z. GitHub then turned their
auto-merge off: "Tried to create or update workflow without `workflows`
permission". Their merge commits would have written workflow text that
neither side held. The GITHUB_TOKEN that `dependabot-auto-merge.yml` arms
with cannot be given that permission, so the merge was refused. #26 was
merged by hand at 19:02Z. Dependabot then rebased #28 onto that master, its
workflow files became its own text on top of master's, and the auto-merge
the same GITHUB_TOKEN armed merged it at 19:21:36Z (2b10d2d, merged by
`github-actions`). So far a bump that edits a workflow has merged itself
whenever its workflow files were up to date with master's: #25, #27, and #28
once rebased. It was refused only when the merge would have combined two
versions of one workflow file.

**Recommended remedy: comment `@dependabot rebase` on the affected bump.**
The rebased bump is armed again by `dependabot-auto-merge.yml`, which runs on
every push to the pull request. The watch names such a bump: auto-merge off
after 6 h, and the bump edits a workflow file. The case is rare. It needs two
workflow-editing pull requests open together, one merging under the other.

**The alternative, not adopted:** arm with a fine-grained token that has
Workflows read and write on webshot-ai. It would be stored as a *Dependabot*
secret, because a run started by Dependabot receives only Dependabot secrets,
not Actions secrets. That fixes the case without a person, and a merge armed
with that token would be the owner's, so push-triggered workflows would run
on it. Its cost is a long-lived credential able to rewrite every workflow in
the repository, available to every Dependabot-triggered run that names it,
to be rotated before it expires, in exchange for one comment on a rare bump.
The decision is the owner's; nothing here creates a token or a secret.

### P84-4 — a hold judged pin by pin

Review of #248: `judge_behind` runs once per pin, but a hold names a package
or an action, not a pin. One name can have two pins: a lock forked by an
environment marker pins two versions of a package, and a bump made in one
workflow and not another pins an action two ways. With one pin behind and
held, and the other current, the current one reported the hold as no longer
needed while the other still needed it. `test_a_hold_on_a_name_with_one_pin_behind_and_one_current_is_still_needed`
and `test_a_hold_on_an_action_pinned_two_ways_is_still_needed` failed on
#248's code (562f857) with exactly that finding. Each pin now only records
whether it is behind, and `run_watch` decides once per name, after every pin
is judged, that a hold is unneeded when none of its pins is behind.

## P27: what MarkItDown's Office readers pass over (2026-10-11)

A slide-text file made from a lecture deck said one slide held only its
title. The lecture video's frame of that slide showed two pairs of hypotheses
written with ≤, > and ≥. WebShot reads `.pptx` and `.docx` through MarkItDown
0.1.8, which reads decks with python-pptx 1.0.2 and Word files with mammoth
1.11.0. Master was 818a9e0. Each case below was measured on a synthetic file
before anything changed. The fixtures are `equation_deck.pptx` and
`equation_report.docx` in `tests/fixtures/office/`, written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`.

### P27-1: a text box holding an equation was dropped whole

The slide's body text box sat in `mc:AlternateContent`. Its
`mc:Choice Requires="a14"` held the text box: 13 `a:t` runs and 3 inline
equations (`a14:m` holding `m:oMath`, whose `m:t` were "≤", ">" and "≥"). Its
`mc:Fallback` held a shape whose only text was a no-break space, filled with a
picture of the rendered text. PowerPoint writes this pair for any text box
with an inline equation in it, so that older readers get the picture.

python-pptx builds its shape tree from the `p:sp`, `p:grpSp`,
`p:graphicFrame`, `p:cxnSp`, `p:pic` and `p:contentPart` children of a slide,
and from nothing else. `mc:AlternateContent` is none of them, so it read
neither branch. MarkItDown rendered the slide as its title alone, and the
manifest had no warning.

### P27-2: the rest of the boundary

| Case | MarkItDown alone | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Text box in `mc:AlternateContent`, Choice `a14` | dropped | read, equations as LaTeX |
| The same inside a group | dropped | read |
| Equation in a shape python-pptx reads | its characters dropped: `a  b` | `a $\ne $ b` |
| Equation in the speaker notes | its characters dropped | read |
| SmartArt, whose words are in `ppt/diagrams/data*.xml` | dropped | read, in the diagram's order |
| A chart python-pptx knows | read as a table | unchanged |
| An Office 2016 chart (`chartex`), an embedded object | nothing | named in a warning |
| Ink and slide transitions, Choice `p14` | nothing | unchanged (P27-4) |
| Word equations | LaTeX, all or none per part | LaTeX, each on its own |
| Word text box holding an equation | read from its VML Fallback | unchanged |
| Word chart, Word SmartArt | dropped | named in a warning, not read |

MarkItDown converts Word's equations itself before mammoth runs: `$…$`
inline, `$$…$$` for a display equation. It converts a whole part inside
`try: … except Exception: pass`. Its converter, `oMath2Latex` (adapted from
dwml), indexes each structure's properties element, and the schema makes
`m:fPr` and `m:dPr` optional. One fraction written without `m:fPr` raised
`KeyError: 'fPr'`, the part reached mammoth unconverted, and mammoth drops
every equation. In the fixture that cost `≠` and `E=mc²` as well as the
fraction. Word writes those elements, so this takes a file from some other
producer. How often that happens was not measured.

### P27-3: the archive is rewritten before MarkItDown opens it

`src/webshot/acquire/ooxml.py` rewrites a deck or a Word file the way
MarkItDown already rewrites a Word file's equations:
- An `mc:AlternateContent` whose Choice needs only DrawingML 2010 (`a14`)
  becomes its Choice. The prefixes in `Requires` are resolved to namespaces,
  not compared as text.
- Each equation becomes a text run of its LaTeX, converted alone.
  The converter is MarkItDown's own, handed in by the bridge, so an equation
  reads the same from a deck as from a Word file. One it refuses becomes its
  characters in document order, and a warning names the slide (or the Word
  part) and those characters.
- A SmartArt frame becomes a text box of its points, read down the `parOf`
  hierarchy from the diagram's root with siblings in `srcOrd` order: the
  outline PowerPoint's text pane shows. A point the hierarchy misses is read
  after the rest.
- A warning names what nothing renders: an embedded object with its
  `progId`, a chart python-pptx cannot read, a table or chart in a Choice that
  stays wrapped, text in such a Choice, and a Word chart or SmartArt diagram.

A slide is parsed only if it contains `AlternateContent`, `oMath` or
`graphicFrame` (a Word part, `oMath` or `graphicData`), and an archive with
nothing rewritten is handed over as the same bytes. A file with none of these
converts exactly as before. Every part goes through defusedxml (spec §6.6).

The first plan gave an equation as its `m:t` characters in document order.
That keeps "≤", but it turns x/2 into `x2` and σ² into `σ2`. LaTeX keeps the
structure and matches what MarkItDown already does for Word, so the
characters became the fallback for an equation the converter refuses.

### P27-4: unwrapping every Choice broke a deck that read before

The first version unwrapped every `mc:AlternateContent`. Over real decks
(P27-5), one that MarkItDown alone read then failed with
`AttributeError: 'lxml.etree._Element' object has no attribute 'has_ph_elm'`.
Its slide held ink: a Choice requiring `p14` that holds a `p:contentPart`.
python-pptx takes that element into its shape tree but has no class for it,
so MarkItDown's first question about the shape raised. Now only a Choice
needing nothing but `a14` is unwrapped. That is ECMA-376 Part 3's rule: take
the first Choice whose namespaces the reader understands. The same decks held
107 Choices requiring `p14` around slide transitions. They stay wrapped too,
and python-pptx never reads transitions.

The bridge no longer trusts its own rewrite either. If MarkItDown cannot read
the rewritten archive, the bridge reads the file as it is and warns that the
text in those structures is missing. A test makes that happen as it happened
here, by letting `p14` through.

### P27-5: real files

Over 23 real decks and 81 Word files, the change gave 26 slides in 5 decks
their missing text (7,705 characters), named 4 embedded objects in 2 decks,
failed on none, and left the output of every Word file as it was. The decks
held 5 `a14` text boxes with 13 equations, 21 SmartArt frames, 2 ink drawings
and 4 embedded objects. None of the Word files had an equation, a chart or a
SmartArt diagram in its body, so the Word half was measured on fixtures only.

### P27-6: what this does not cover

- Word SmartArt and charts are named, not read. Reading Word SmartArt would
  take the same data-model walk; it is not done here.
- A picture stays MarkItDown's `![name](name.jpg)`, so text that exists only
  as a picture (a Fallback, a pasted screenshot) is not read.
- An Equation Editor 3.0 object is an embedded object: named, not read.
- mammoth reads no header or footer, equations or not.

### P27-7: the tests

`tests/test_ooxml.py` holds the archive-level cases, which need nothing but
the standard library: a file with nothing to rewrite comes back as the same
bytes, nested Choices, ink left wrapped, a prefix bound to another namespace,
hostile and malformed parts, frames left wrapped. With the office extra it
holds each fixture's exact Markdown and warnings, the fallback to the file as
it is, Word output that matches MarkItDown's wherever MarkItDown converted
every equation, and a test that pins MarkItDown alone still losing this text,
so an upgrade that starts reading it says so. `tests/test_office_formats.py`
captures both fixtures end to end and finds each warning in the manifest.

## P28: a document's text was written into the page as markup (2026-10-11)

A deck whose text box read `<img src="https://tracker.invalid/beacon.png"> and
*stars*` rendered, through `materialize_source`, as
`<p><img src="https://tracker.invalid/beacon.png"> and <em>stars</em></p>`.
MarkItDown's deck reader appends a shape's text to its Markdown as it is,
Python-Markdown passes raw HTML through, and `MARKDOWN_POLICY` allows
`img[src]`: P8-9's class, which `_escape_cell` had closed for CSV cells alone.
Measured with MarkItDown 0.1.8, python-pptx 1.0.2, mammoth 1.11.0, markdownify
1.2.3, Python-Markdown 3.10.3 and nh3 0.3.7, on master dd961c3 (P27 merged).
The fixtures are the five `markup_*` files in `tests/fixtures/office/`, written
by `tools/fixtures/office.py`; every host in them is `.invalid`.

### P28-1: the capture fetched what the text named

A local file is captured with no request gate unless `--block-private-requests`
or MCP roots install one, and that gate passes public hosts. With a local
server standing in for the tracker, one default capture of each payload file
requested: from a deck, 7 URLs (its title, body text, a Markdown image in the
body, a table cell, a chart's title and category, the notes); from a Word file
3; from a workbook 2; from an EPUB 4 (body, a Markdown image, `dc:title`,
`dc:description`), besides the book's own `<img>`; from a zip 8, half of them
from a deck inside it. A request that succeeds leaves no trace in the manifest
or the report. One to a host that does not resolve shows as "N requests for
the page's resources failed (image N)", with the URLs in `--report` only.

### P28-2: what Python-Markdown made of the rest

| Text in the document | Rendered before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `<img src=…>`, `<b>x</b>`, `<class '…'>` | an element; an unknown tag dropped with its name | the text |
| `*x*`, `__init__`, `_____` | emphasis; the underscores lost | the text |
| `# x`, and `#hashtag` with no space | a heading (one became a deck's page title) | the text |
| `C#` in a heading line | `C`: trailing hashes are stripped | `C#` |
| `3. Third` | a list, renumbered from 1: `ol[start]` is not in the policy | the text |
| `Total` over `===`, `Term` over `: x` | a heading; a definition list | the text |
| `~~~` or ```` ``` ```` alone on a line | a fence that swallowed what followed | the text |
| `[id]: url`, `*[HTML]: …`, `Set {x}` | the line removed; `{x}` taken as attributes | the text |
| `a\*b`, `C:\Users\_x_` | a backslash escaping what follows it | the text |
| `&copy;` typed as such | © | `&copy;` |
| a tab or four spaces after a blank line | a code block | the text |
| `robots!` and then a link | an image (the `!` joins markdownify's `[`) | the text and the link |
| alt text `x](https://…/a.png) ![y` | a second image, fetched | one image's alt |
| a link target `…?q=)![y](https://…/b.png` | a link cut short and an image | one link, `()` encoded |
| a `<pre>` holding a ```` ``` ```` line | the block closed; what followed read as Markdown | one block |

### P28-3: where MarkItDown takes a document's text

| Format | Written into Markdown as it is | Written through markdownify |
|---|---|---|
| `.pptx` | shape and title text, notes, a chart's title, categories and series | table cells |
| `.docx` | nothing | all of it, alt text and link targets included |
| `.xlsx` | sheet names, as `## name` | cells |
| `.epub` | `dc:` metadata, as `**Title:** …` | chapters, alt, links, `<pre>` |
| `.zip` | member names, and every member its plain-text reader takes | each member's own reader |
| `.csv` | cells, after `_escape_cell` | nothing |

markdownify is no defence: the HTML mammoth and pandas write is escaped, but
BeautifulSoup decodes it and markdownify escapes only `*` and `_`. Its
`escape_misc` aims at CommonMark: Python-Markdown prints `\=` and reads `\<img>`
as a backslash and a tag. A pptx table cell went through `html.escape` and back
out the same way. A CSV inside a zip skipped `_escape_cell` entirely, and a TSV
there was not a table. And `_escape_cell` itself was wrong three ways for this
renderer: `=SUM(A1)` printed as `\=SUM(A1)` and `~x` as `\~x`, a trailing
`{x}` was dropped, and a cell's own backslash escaped what followed it.

### P28-4: written as character references

Each string a document contributes is encoded where it enters Markdown: `&`,
`<` and `>` as named references, and Markdown's characters as numeric ones,
which the browser reads as the character and Markdown as nothing. nh3 writes
the character back when it serializes the page, so text that needed none of
this renders byte for byte as before, the heading anchors `toc` derives
included. `! # * [ \ ] _ ` { | }` are encoded wherever they stand, `+ - : = ~`,
an ordered list's full stop and code-block indentation where a line begins.
A test holds that set to Python-Markdown's own list of escapable characters.

Backslash escapes were rejected: no backslash escapes `=`, `~` or `:` there,
and markdownify escapes `*` again, so a deck's table cell would have printed
`\*`. Turning raw HTML off in the renderer was rejected too: MarkItDown writes
HTML of its own (`<!-- Slide number -->`, markdownify's `<u>`, the CSV `<br>`).

The first version encoded every punctuation character. A 1.7 MB CSV then took
5.4 s instead of 3.2 s, and a 6.8 MB zip of 1,075 Python files 33 s instead of
9 s, all in Python-Markdown's inline pass, which stashes each reference on its
own. Narrowing the set to the above made the CSV level; the zip still took
28 s against 15 s in that run, on 1.4 million references in prose. So a zip
member read as plain text became a fenced code block, as a top-level `.txt`
is: literal by construction, lines intact, and nothing to encode. A table cell
or a heading gets no line-start encoding either, since markdownify writes each
as one line after its own marker; every negative number in a sheet had been a
reference, and six workbooks 12% slower.

### P28-5: where it is applied

- **markdownify.** `_TextMarkdownify` replaces its `escape`, fences a `<pre>`
  longer than any backtick run in it, and is handed a tree whose alt and title
  attributes are encoded and whose `href`, `src`, `data-src` and `poster` have
  whitespace, `()<>`, quotes, backticks and `\` percent-encoded.
  `_TextHtmlConverter` copies `HtmlConverter.convert`, because upstream names
  its writer inside that method; it also encodes the plain text its
  too-deep fallback returns, which upstream writes raw. The Word, Excel and
  EPUB readers write through it, set on their `_html_converter`; a release
  without that attribute is refused at construction.
- **Text written straight in.** A deck's slide, notes and chart parts and a
  workbook's sheet names are encoded in the archive before the reader opens it
  (`ooxml.rewrite_parts`, by content type, through defusedxml). An EPUB's
  metadata is encoded as it is read, and the title the bridge returns is
  decoded again for the page's `<title>`. A zip is walked by the bridge: names
  encoded, a CSV or TSV escaped as a top-level one is, Markdown and notebooks
  rendered as Markdown, anything else as a code block.
- **In place.** When a converter raises, MarkItDown tries the next that
  accepts the file, so a builtin left beside its replacement would read a deck
  the replacement refused, text raw. Each is replaced at its own position and
  priority. A deck whose notes part declares an entity now ends after one
  attempt, with exit 2.

P27's equation LaTeX passes through intact: `$\leq $` is written as
`$&#92;leq $` and renders as it did, and both P27 fixtures render byte for
byte as before.

### P28-6: real files

Over 178 real files (23 decks, 81 Word files, 6 workbooks, 1 EPUB, 5 zips, 62
CSVs), the page of 151 was byte-identical and 3 failed as before, on archive
limits. Each of the 27 that changed had text that had been read as markup:
Python comments pasted into Word files, which had become headings, and pasted
`df.info()` output whose `<class '…DataFrame'>` line had vanished as a tag;
`1.`/`2.` typed as paragraphs, which had become lists numbered from 1 even
where the first was `2.`; a hashtag on a deck's last slide, which had become
the page's title; `_____` blanks for answers, turned into bold and italics; a
published book whose "…robots!" and footnote link had become a broken image,
and whose chapter summaries a definition list; `*all*` typed on a slide; an
`&amp;` typed into a citation; number grids indented with tabs, which had
become code blocks; and a zipped Python project whose `.py` files had read as
Markdown. Conversion took, before and after, 10.59 s and 10.90 s for the 62
CSVs, 7.83 s and 7.85 s for the Word files, 25.26 s and 25.78 s for the
workbooks, 8.52 s and 9.63 s for the zips, and 1.47 s and 1.96 s for the decks,
whose parts are now parsed and written again.

### P28-7: what this does not cover

- A `.md` file is Markdown, in a zip or not: its raw HTML is its author's,
  rendered and sanitized as before, and an image it names is fetched. So is an
  EPUB's own `<img src="https://…">`, as an HTML file's would be. Nothing gates
  a local capture's requests; this keeps a document's *text* from making them.
- P27's rewrite does not reach a deck or a Word file inside a zip. P29
  closes this.
- `ol[start]` is not in `MARKDOWN_POLICY`, so a real list that starts at 3 is
  still numbered from 1. P30 closes this.
- A picture is still MarkItDown's `![name](name.jpg)`, a `file:` request that
  fails (P27-6).

### P28-8: the tests

`tests/test_office_markup.py` holds the encoded set to Python-Markdown's
escapable characters; renders 22 strings and 10 cells as themselves; checks
that text needing no encoding renders byte for byte as before; reads each
`markup_*` fixture and finds no element its text could have made and every
line of it as text; checks the EPUB title round trip, that no replaced
converter is left registered, that a refused deck ends after one attempt, that
the copied HTML converter renders as upstream's on plain documents, and the
too-deep fallback. `tests/test_office_formats.py` captures the five fixtures
end to end and asserts no request failed. P27-7's exact-Markdown tests now
compare the Markdown with its references read back, which still pins every
character, and fails if one is written twice.

## P29: a deck or Word file inside a zip skipped P27's rewrite (2026-10-11)

P28-7 recorded that P27's rewrite reached a deck or a Word file on its own
and not one inside a zip. The bridge's zip converter, added in P28, handed
each member straight to MarkItDown, so a member got neither `ooxml`'s rewrite
nor its fallback. Measured on P28's branch at e62ea59, before it merged, with
the package versions P28 names. The fixture is
`equation_archive.zip` in `tests/fixtures/office/`, written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`: P27's two fixtures, byte for byte, as
`slides/equation_deck.pptx` and `reports/equation_report.docx`.

### P29-1: what a zipped deck and Word file lost

| Text | On its own | In a zip, before | Now |
|---|---|---|---|
| The wrapped text box: sentinel, `x ≤ 12; y1 > 7` | read | dropped | read |
| The grouped box's `z ≥ 3` | read | dropped | read |
| A bare equation, `a ≠ b` | read | `a  b` | read |
| The notes' equation | read | dropped | read |
| SmartArt's two steps | read | dropped | read |
| A refused equation's characters, `a+b` | read, with a warning | dropped | read, with a warning |
| The Word file's four equations | read | dropped | read |
| The Word chart, the embedded object | named | not named | named |

The deck lost 8 of the lines it has on its own (157 characters) and the Word
file 5 (56 characters). The archive had no warnings, where the two files on
their own have five.

### P29-2: one path for a file and a member

`_convert_bytes` holds what a file and a member share: the CSV escape, the
rewrite, the conversion, the fallback to the bytes as they were, and the
warnings each leaves. `to_markdown` turns its failure into the user's error.
`_member_markdown` fences plain text as before, and the zip converter decides
what a member's failure costs. So a member is read by no path the file is
not. A member's warnings come back with its path in front:
`slides/equation_deck.pptx: Slide 5: an embedded object (Equation.3) is not in
the page.` MarkItDown's result has no field for warnings, but it returns the
object a converter made, so the zip converter returns a subclass that carries
them. A zip inside a zip hands its own up, and the outer one names both:
`inner.zip: deck.pptx: Slide 5: …`.

The fallback warning began with the file's name. With a member's path in front
it would have named the file twice, so it now begins "The file could not be
read once its equations…" for a file on its own too.

### P29-3: a member whose part WebShot refuses

`ooxml` raises `ValueError` for a part that declares an entity (spec §6.6) or
that the member's own archive cannot give up. Before, the same refusal came
from P28's `rewrite_parts` inside MarkItDown's deck reader, so the zip
converter saw a failed conversion and left the member out without a word. Now
it is raised before the reader runs, where the zip converter can tell a
refusal from a reader's failure. The member is still left out and the rest of
the archive still read, and a warning names the member and the reason: `hostile.pptx is not in the page:
ppt/slides/slide1.xml declares XML entities or external references, which
WebShot refuses to parse (…)`. A file on its own refused the same way still
ends the run with exit 2.

### P29-4: real files

None of the 5 zips in the Google Drive `School` folder holds a deck or a Word
file, so each of its 23 decks and 81 Word files was also read wrapped alone in
a zip. Every file in the folder's P28-6 set (178: those 109, 6 workbooks, 1
EPUB and 62 CSVs) rendered to the same page with the same warnings as P28's
merged head, d46f5f1, byte for byte; the same 3 fail in both, on archive
limits. Wrapped, each member's Markdown is now its file's, and its warnings
are the file's under the member's path. Before, the wrapped decks lost the
text of 26 slides in 5 decks (7,705 characters, what P27-5 restored to the
same decks on their own) and their 4 embedded-object warnings. The wrapped
Word files lost nothing, since none has an equation, a chart or SmartArt in
its body (P27-5). No wrapped file failed. Timing was not measured to a useful
precision: the machine's load average was over 400, and the six workbooks,
whose path this does not touch, took 26 s and 231 s in two runs of the same
code.

### P29-5: what this does not cover

- A member nothing reads, or whose reader fails on its bytes as they were too,
  is still left out without a word: MarkItDown's choice, which P28 kept.
  Saying so means deciding what to say for directory entries and `__MACOSX/`
  copies, and wording a missing extra for a member as `_conversion_error`
  words it for a file. P33 closes this.

### P29-6: the tests

`tests/test_ooxml.py` holds `equation_archive.zip`'s exact Markdown and
warnings, finds each member's Markdown verbatim inside the zip's, and follows
the warnings through `materialize_source`. It also checks that a zip inside a
zip names both, that a member gets the fallback and says so, that a member
with a refused part is left out and named while its neighbour is read, and
that a zip with no Office member has no warning.
`tests/test_office_formats.py` captures the archive end to end. It finds the
deck's sentinel, which sits in the wrapped text box, and the five warnings in
the manifest under their members' names.

## P30: the number a list starts at (2026-10-11)

P28-7 recorded that `MARKDOWN_POLICY` does not allow `ol[start]`, so a list
that starts at 3 in a local document was numbered from 1 on its page.
Measured with Python-Markdown 3.10.3, MarkItDown 0.1.8, markdownify 1.2.3,
mammoth 1.11.0, nh3 0.3.7, docling-slim 2.132.0 and Chromium 153.0.8010.12, on
master 34d9f06. The fixtures are `tests/fixtures/numbered_lists.md`,
`tests/fixtures/office/numbered_book.epub` (written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`) and `tests/fixtures/list_numbering.html`.

### P30-1: what each path did

| Input | What reaches Python-Markdown | Page before | Page now |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.md`, a list beginning `3.` | the file | `<ol>` | `<ol start="3">` |
| `.md`, a list beginning `0.`; one nested, beginning `7.` | the file | `<ol>` | `<ol start="0">`; `<ol start="7">` |
| EPUB `<ol start="5">`, and nested `<ol start="4">` | `5.`, `4.` from markdownify | `<ol>` | `<ol start="5">`, `<ol start="4">` |
| EPUB `<ol start="-2">` | `1.`: markdownify reads a start only where `isnumeric()` holds | `<ol>` | `<ol>` |
| EPUB `<ol reversed start="3">` | `3.`, `4.`: markdownify counts up | `<ol>` | `<ol start="3">`, counting up |
| `.docx`, a list Word starts at 4 (`w:startOverride`) or 3 (`w:start`), or continues past a paragraph | `1.`: mammoth writes `<ol>` | `<ol>` | `<ol>` |

Python-Markdown writes the first item's digits as they are (`03.` becomes
`start="03"`); the page then carries the number, below.

### P30-2: the snapshot kept whatever the page wrote

`SNAPSHOT_POLICY` is built on nh3's defaults, which allow `ol[start]`, so a
page's own value reached `content.html` as written. docling's HTML backend
takes it where `str.isnumeric()` holds and reads it with `int()`:

| A page's `start` | Chromium numbers the list from | `content.md` said |
|---|---|---|
| `²` | 1 | nothing: the capture exited 8, "docling could not parse the snapshot: invalid literal for int()" |
| `٣` (Arabic-Indic three) | 1 | 3 |
| `99999999999` | 1 | 99999999999 |
| `3abc`, `+3`, `\t3` | 3 | 1 |
| `-2` | -2 | 1 |

So one character in a page's markup failed the whole capture, and in the other
rows the record and the page disagreed about a number a reader saw.

### P30-3: what Chromium reads from the attribute

HTML's rules for parsing integers, then a signed 32-bit range: leading ASCII
whitespace is skipped, one `+` or `-` is taken, ASCII digits are read, and
whatever follows them is ignored (`3abc`, `3.5` and `0x10` read as 3, 3 and 0).
No digits, a no-break or figure space before them, a non-ASCII digit, or a
value outside -2147483648 to 2147483647 reads as no number, and the list starts
at 1. `CHROMIUM_READS` in the tests is the table, and a browser test reads
`ol.start` from Chromium for the fixture page, so a disagreement fails rather
than drifting.

### P30-4: the change

`sanitize.py` keeps `ol[start]` as the number Chromium reads, written as plain
decimal, and drops it where Chromium reads none, through nh3's
`attribute_filter`. It is applied in `sanitize()`, so both documents share it,
as they share the URL schemes: a local document's page is captured, and its
snapshot sanitized again. `MARKDOWN_POLICY` now allows the attribute;
`SNAPSHOT_EXTRA_ATTRIBUTES` names it, so it is no longer held only by an
upstream default that could shrink.

Spec §6.5 is unaffected: `start` is not a URL or a handler, and its value can
only be `-?[0-9]+`. The filter is called for every allowed attribute: on a
9.9 MB synthetic snapshot with 360,000 of them, sanitizing took 0.38 s instead
of 0.28 s (best of three), with identical output.

The filter must not raise, because nh3 does not refuse an attribute whose
filter raised. It reports the exception as unraisable and keeps the attribute
as written: a filter that fails, fails open. The first version passed every
run of digits to `int()`, which raises past 4,300 digits on Python 3.12. A
`start` of 5,000 ones therefore reached the snapshot whole, and docling's own
`int()` failed the capture with exit 8, as `²` had. The review of #179 found
the raise. `html_integer` now strips leading zeros and refuses more than ten
digits before converting. Chromium agrees: it reads 5,000 ones as no number,
5,000 zeros and a 7 as 7, and 5,000 zeros after a minus sign and before a 2
as -2.

### P30-5: real files

Over 231 real files (53 Markdown files, 81 Word files, 23 decks, 6 workbooks,
1 EPUB, 5 zips, 62 CSVs), 228 rendered and 3 failed as before, on archive
limits. The page of 6 changed, and in each the only change was a `start` on an
`<ol>`, 9 lists in all. One was a Markdown README whose list begins at 4. The
other 8 were in 3 Word files and 2 decks, where a paragraph typed as `2.` or
`3.` had been read as a list: before, each read 1; now each reads the number
typed. Those runs were on master before P28 merged. With P28 merged, the six
files were rendered again: the five Word files and decks have no `start` and
show the typed numbers as text, and the README's list still begins at 4.
Rendering all 231 took 57.9 s before and 60.8 s after, one run each.

### P30-6: what this does not cover

- **Word numbering.** mammoth's numbering model holds a level and whether it
  is ordered, no start, so every Word list is numbered from 1 and a list Word
  continues past a paragraph restarts. Carrying it would take reading
  `numbering.xml` beside mammoth.
- **Two adjacent lists.** Python-Markdown reads two lists with nothing between
  them as one: markdownify's `5. Fifth` followed by an `<ol>` of its own,
  `1. One`, became one list numbered 5 and 6. `numbered_book.epub` closes
  each list with a paragraph for that reason. P32 closes this.
- **`reversed`, `type` and `li[value]`.** Neither allowlist keeps them, and
  docling reads none, so a list counting down is recorded counting up and a
  lettered list as numbered. markdownify writes a negative start as 1, and
  docling numbers one from 1 in `content.md` though `content.html` keeps it.

### P30-7: the tests

`tests/test_list_numbering.py` holds `html_integer` to the table Chromium was
measured against and both allowlists to the same table, 5,000-digit values
included. Property tests, over short text and over long runs of digits (up to
6,000 leading zeros and 6,309 more digits),
check that `html_integer` returns None or an in-range number, that a kept
`start` is only ever a plain 32-bit integer, and that sanitizing again changes
nothing. The `²` and 5,000-digit snapshots that failed now extract. The two local
fixtures are rendered and their lists' openings compared, and both are
captured end to end and their numbers found in `content.md`. A browser test
loads `list_numbering.html`, reads `ol.start` for each of its 20 lists from
Chromium, and requires the snapshot to keep exactly those numbers and
`content.md` to list each first item under it, a negative start excepted
(P30-6). `tests/test_office_formats.py` captures `numbered_book.epub` with the
other fixtures.

## P31: Word's list numbers, which mammoth does not read (2026-10-11)

P30-6 left Word lists numbered from 1: mammoth's numbering model holds a list
item's level and whether it is ordered, never its number, so every `<ol>` it
writes is bare. Measured with mammoth 1.11.0, MarkItDown 0.1.8, markdownify
1.2.3, Python-Markdown 3.10.3 and Beautiful Soup 4.15.0, on master 18229fe
with P30 (#179) and P32 merged, and against Microsoft Word 16.113.3 for Mac.
Word's numbers were read with AppleScript, as `list value` and `list string`
of each paragraph's `list format`, from 34 `.docx` files built by hand to
hold one case each; 32 of them are `WORD_SHOWS` in
`tests/test_word_lists.py`, and the other two its own tests. The fixture is
`tests/fixtures/office/numbered_report.docx`, written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`, and Word shows on it exactly the numbers its
test pins.

### P31-1: what the page showed

| A Word list | Word shows | mammoth wrote | Page before | Page now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `w:start` 3 | 3, 4 | `<ol>` | 1, 2 | 3, 4 |
| `w:start` absent | 0, 1 | `<ol>` | 1, 2 | 0, 1 |
| `w:startOverride` 4, and an item after a paragraph | 4, 5, 6 | `<ol>`, `<ol>` | 1, 2, 1 | 4, 5, 6 |
| going on past a paragraph | 1, 2, 3 | `<ol>`, `<ol>` | 1, 2, 1 | 1, 2, 3 |
| two `w:num` of one definition, a paragraph between | 1, 2, 3, 4 | `<ol>`, `<ol>` | 1, 2, 1, 2 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| two definitions, nothing between | 1, 2, 1, 2 | one `<ol>` | 1, 2, 3, 4 | 1, 2, 1, 2 |
| an empty item between two | 1, 2, 3 | one `<ol>`, the empty item dropped | 1, 2 | 1, 3 |
| numbered by its paragraph style, `w:start` 5 | 5, 6 | `<ol>` | 1, 2 | 5, 6 |
| items in a table between items outside it | 1, 2, 3, 4 | `<ol>` each side, one in the cell | 1; `1. … 2. …` in the cell; 1 | 1; `2. … 3. …`; 4 |
| `lowerLetter` from 3 | c, d | `<ol>` | 1, 2 | 3, 4 |
| `numFmt` `none` | no number | `<ol>` | 1, 2 | 1, 2, and a warning |
| a heading numbered as a list | 1 | `<h1>` | no number | no number, and a warning |

A list in a table cell is text in the cell, because markdownify writes a cell
on one line; its numbers are now Word's. A lettered or Roman list is shown in
digits with Word's ordinal, as P30-6 leaves `type` out.

### P31-2: how Word counts

ISO/IEC 29500-1 §17.9 describes most of this, and Word was measured on every
rule below rather than trusted to it:

- **Every `w:num` that uses one abstract definition counts on one set of
  counters.** Two instances with a paragraph between them number 1, 2, 3, 4,
  not 1, 2, 1, 2; three of them, two with overrides, number 1, 10, 20, 21,
  22, 23 in the order their items come. Two definitions count apart.
- **A `w:startOverride` sets its level's count at the first item of that
  instance at that level**, and is the level's start for that instance from
  then on: a restarted level comes back to it (§17.9.27). An override of one
  level leaves the instance counting on the others with the rest. A
  `w:lvlOverride` without one changes nothing, and Word does not take the
  start of an override's own `w:lvl`.
- **`w:start` absent is 0** (§17.9.26), and Word counts from 0. A negative
  start is counted from, but Word shows no number on any item of that level.
- **Using a level restarts every deeper level** unless its `w:lvlRestart` says
  otherwise: 0 never, and *n* only when a level above *n* is used (§17.9.11).
- **A deeper level used first counts each level above it as used**, at its
  start: items at level 1, then one at level 0, number a, b, 2. A level
  `numbering.xml` does not define does the same, and shows nothing.
- `numFmt` `none` counts and shows no number. An empty numbered paragraph keeps
  its number. A paragraph in a table counts in document order. A `w:numPr`
  with no `w:ilvl` is level 0. A paragraph style's `w:numPr` numbers its
  paragraphs, and a style based on it (`w:basedOn`) numbers its own on the
  same count; `w:numId` 0 on a paragraph takes the numbering away. A
  definition that names a numbering style (`w:numStyleLink`) counts with the
  definition that style's list uses.
- A `w:numId` that `numbering.xml` does not define shows `1.` in Word;
  mammoth reads no list there, so the page shows a paragraph.

### P31-3: the change

`ooxml.number_word_lists` reads `numbering.xml`, `styles.xml` and the body
through defusedxml, by namespace, and counts every numbered paragraph by the
rules above in the order mammoth reads them: an `mc:AlternateContent`'s
Fallback, not its Choice, and a paragraph whose mark is a tracked deletion as
part of the next, as mammoth does (that one was not measured in Word). Each
paragraph Word numbers with an ordered format gets a text run at its head: a
private-use character, the first 16 hex digits of the archive's SHA-256, its
index, and a closing private-use character. No document's text can hold the
mark of the archive it is in, and the same file is marked the same way twice. A list whose
start is no number is left unmarked. A file with no paragraph to mark goes to
mammoth byte for byte.

The bridge's HTML step, given the numbers as the `word_lists` option
MarkItDown hands its Word reader's HTML converter, owns each `<li>` its first
mark, starts each `<ol>` at its first item's number, splits it where the
numbers stop running on, and takes every mark out before markdownify. A mark
that was all its paragraph held stands for one mammoth would have dropped as
empty: it goes, its item with it, and its number splits the list. The split
lists stand side by side and rely on P32 to stay apart. What cannot be
carried is left as mammoth wrote it and counted for the manifest: an `<ol>`
with an item that holds no mark, one with an item Word shows no number on,
and a mark no list item owns, which is a paragraph Word numbers that the page
does not show as a list item. mammoth's own footnote and endnote lists are
left alone.

The step runs in `_convert_bytes`, so a Word file inside a zip is numbered
too (P29), and its warnings are named for the member. A marked file mammoth
cannot open is read as it is, with a warning, as P27's rewrite is. Numbers
that never reach the HTML step raise: they would leave the marks in the text
and number nothing.

`_rebuild` stores the members it copies instead of deflating them again. The
archive is read once, in memory, and with every Word file that has a list now
rewritten, recompressing its pictures cost 0.32 to 0.60 s on 3 to 6 MB files;
stored, 0.025 to 0.056 s. This applies to P27's and P28's rewrites as well;
what the readers see of each part is unchanged.

### P31-4: real files

All 82 real `.docx` files rendered, before and after. 30 hold a paragraph
Word numbers in an ordered format. Word read 483 such items with text in
them; 216 were shown with Word's number before and 327 now. Of the other 156:

- 106 are nested items that the page lists in their parent's list, because
  markdownify indents a nested list by its marker's width (3 spaces under
  `1.`) and Python-Markdown needs 4. That is its own defect, outside this
  change (P40).
- 39 are numbered headings, in 5 files, which the page shows without a
  number; each of those files now says so in a warning.
- 11 the comparison did not match by text, and are shown with Word's numbers:
  5 items whose text has no-break spaces in it, and 6 lists inside table
  cells.

The page of 5 files changed. 17 lines are an `<ol>` gaining a `start`; in
one of the 5, 19 questions numbered past 9 also have their answer choices
nested under them now, as three lines each, because a marker of `10.` is 4
characters wide and its nested list is indented far enough for
Python-Markdown. Their words are the same, and the questions numbered below
10 are flattened as before. No page lost or gained a word, and the
manifest of 5 files gained the numbered-heading warning. Converting all 82
took 13.04 s before and 12.53 s after, the best of three runs per file.

Timed again when this entry merged with the other acquire entries of
2026-10-17 (P77-4 describes the copy), over the 120 Word files that render,
in three alternating rounds at a load average near 40. The best of three per
file sums to 31.1 s on master and 33.9 s with this change, 9% more, about
23 ms a file, and every round was slower with it. `number_word_lists` alone
takes 1.05 s of that, best of three, and rewrites 38 of the 120; where the
rest goes was not traced. With all five entries the sum is 34.2 s. In three
alternating rounds of all five against master, as the load average fell from
about 150 to about 30, the EPUB, the zips and the workbooks were no slower,
best of three: 1.10 s and 1.10 s, 37.0 s and 34.7 s, 30.2 s and 29.8 s. So
the figure above is not what this change costs on master now.

### P31-5: what this does not cover

- **Nested lists.** Each nested `<ol>` gets its number. When P31-4 was
  measured, Python-Markdown flattened one into its parent unless the
  parent's marker was 4 characters wide, and a sublist of bullets became
  text in its parent item; P40 has since kept nested lists nested. Rendered
  again with P40, when this entry merged with the other acquire entries of
  2026-10-17 (P77-4 describes the copy): in the real Word files 57 list
  items, in 6 files, hold a numbered list of their own, each nested on the
  page. For each, the number worked out for its first item is 1, so none
  takes a `start`, and no item is one whose number could not be worked out.
  The 5 files P31-4 names still change, by the same 17 starts, and the same 5
  gain the numbered-heading warning.
- **A numbered heading, and a list Word shows no number on**, are said in
  warnings, not shown as Word shows them.
- **The rest of a label.** `type` (letters, Roman numerals) is dropped as
  P30-6 records, and `w:lvlText` is not carried: `Step %1:`, `1.1` and
  `(a)` all show as a number and a full stop.
- **Lists outside the body.** Footnotes, endnotes and comments are not
  counted; a list there keeps mammoth's numbering, and its items count as
  ones that could not be numbered. A text box's paragraphs are counted where
  the box is anchored, which was not measured against Word.
- **A `w:numId` with no definition** (P31-2), which Word numbers and mammoth
  does not read as a list. **Tracked changes** are counted as mammoth reads
  them: a paragraph's current properties, and a deleted paragraph mark
  joining its paragraph to the next.

### P31-6: the tests

`tests/test_word_lists.py` builds each of the 32 measured cases and requires
`number_word_lists` to give Word's number for every ordered item, in order,
and to mark exactly those paragraphs; then, as measured, a numbering-style
link and a style based on a numbered one; and a style link that loops, a start that is no number, a file with nothing to number, a
Fallback counted once, a deleted paragraph mark, a document written with
`ns0:` prefixes as `prepare_docx` leaves one, and a mark that is the file's
own. The HTML step is held on mammoth-shaped markup: a start, a list left as
written when it starts at 1, a split, an empty item, a nested list, each of
the three counts, mammoth's notes, and text that looks like another file's
mark. Through MarkItDown, the fixture's Markdown lists `NUMBERED_PAGE` and
its two warnings, on its own and inside a zip; mammoth alone still numbers
from 1; a marked file mammoth cannot open falls back; and a `word_lists`
dropped on the way fails. `tests/test_office_formats.py` captures the fixture
with the other office fixtures and requires `content.md` to list
`NUMBERED_PAGE` under Word's numbers, with the warnings in the manifest.

## P32: two lists side by side became one (2026-10-11)

P30-6 recorded that an EPUB's `<ol start="5"><li>Fifth</li></ol>` followed by
`<ol><li>One</li></ol>` reached the page as one list numbered 5 and 6.
markdownify writes two adjacent lists with a blank line between them, and
Python-Markdown reads a list of the same kind after a blank line as the first
one going on. Measured with MarkItDown 0.1.8, markdownify 1.2.3, mammoth
1.11.0, Python-Markdown 3.10.3 (`extra`, `sane_lists`, `toc`), nh3 0.3.7,
docling-slim 2.132.0 and Chromium 153.0.8010.12, on fix/office-text-as-text
d46f5f1 (P28, whose `_TextMarkdownify` is where this lands). The fixture is
`tests/fixtures/office/adjacent_lists_book.epub`, written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`; its words are made up.

### P32-1: which inputs reach it

Each input was converted by the bridge and rendered as the adapter renders it.
"Loose" is Python-Markdown wrapping an item in `<p>`, which it does to the
items either side of a blank line inside what it takes for one list.

| Input | markdownify wrote | Page before | Page now |
|---|---|---|---|
| EPUB `<ol start="5">` then `<ol>` | `5. Fifth`, blank, `1. One` | one `<ol>`, numbered 5 and 6, both loose | two, tight |
| EPUB two `<ol>`s of two items | `1.`, `2.`, blank, `1.`, `2.` | one `<ol>` of four; the middle two loose | two, tight |
| EPUB `<ul>` then `<ul>`; three `<ul>`s; six one-item `<ol>`s | the same shape | one list each time | one per list |
| the same, with whitespace, an empty `<div>`, `<p>`, `<a id>`, `<ol>` or `<li>`, `<p>&nbsp;</p>`, `<p><br/></p>`, a comment or `<br/>` between | exactly what nothing between writes | one list | two |
| each list in a `<div>` of its own, or only the second | the same | one list | two |
| both in one `<blockquote>` | `> 1. A`, `>`, `> 1. B` | one list | two |
| both in one `<dd>` | `:   1. A`, blank, `    1. B` | one list | two |
| a chapter ending with a list, the next beginning with one | each chapter on its own; MarkItDown joins them with a blank line | one list | two |
| an HTML file in a zip with two `<ol>`s | as EPUB | one list | two |
| `<ol>` then `<ul>`, `<ul>` then `<ol>` | blank line between | two: `sane_lists` | unchanged |
| text, a paragraph, `<hr>`, an image, a heading, or a quotation holding only the second list, between | that block | two | unchanged |
| both in a `<pre>`; both in a table cell | a code block; one cell line | code; text | unchanged |
| two lists nested in one item | `* Parent`, `  + Child one`, `  + Child two` | flattened (P32-5) | unchanged |
| Word: two numbered (or two bulleted) lists with different `numId`s, or with an empty paragraph between | mammoth writes one `<ol>` (`<ul>`) | one list | unchanged (P31) |
| Word: numbered then bulleted, bulleted then numbered, numbered, bulleted, numbered | `<ol>`, `<ul>`, … | separate lists | unchanged |

A workbook's cells and a deck's tables go through markdownify too, as tables;
MarkItDown writes a deck's text itself. Neither holds a list.

In `content.md` the merged lists were one run of items: `3. Dulvane` followed
`2. Crindet` where the book's second list begins at 1, and two bulleted lists
had no blank line between them. Twelve of the fixture's items were loose in
`content.html`.

### P32-2: what keeps two lists apart

| Between two lists in the Markdown | Page |
|---|---|
| a blank line, as markdownify writes | one list, the items at the seam loose |
| two blank lines | the same |
