| `<!-- -->` on a line of its own, with or without blank lines round it | two lists, tight; nh3 removes the comment, leaving whitespace between `</ol>` and `<ol>` |
| `<div></div>` | two lists; nh3 removes the `div` |
| in a blockquote, `> <!-- -->` between `>` lines | two lists |
| in a definition, the comment indented four spaces | two lists |
| the comment indented four spaces after a top-level item | it joins that item: one list, loose |

The comment adds no element and no text. Captured end to end, the fixture's
`content.md`, `content.html` and `content.txt` hold no `<!--`, and in every
case in P32-1 the page's text, whitespace aside, is upstream's.

### P32-3: the change

`_TextMarkdownify.convert_list` marks where each list it writes begins and
ends, unless the list sits in an item, a table cell, a heading or a `<pre>`.
The marks go inside the list's leading and trailing newlines, which
markdownify counts to collapse the blank lines between blocks. Whether
anything stands between two lists is known only once the Markdown is written,
so the marks are resolved when it is whole: `<!-- -->` goes where one list's
end meets the start of another of the same kind with only blank lines between,
on a line of its own at the second list's indentation (`> ` in a quotation,
four spaces in a definition), and every mark is removed. Where the blank lines
between carry other indentation the two are in different blocks, which
Markdown keeps apart already, and nothing is added. Each mark holds a token
drawn per conversion between private-use characters, so a document's own text,
a `<pre>`'s included, cannot hold one, and its own private-use characters are
kept.

`_TextHtmlConverter` resolves each document as markdownify finishes it, except
for EPUB: `_TextEpubConverter` shares one set of marks across its chapters and
resolves the book once MarkItDown has joined them. A `.md` file never reaches
the bridge and renders as before: two lists with a blank line between are one
list there, as Markdown says.

### P32-4: real files

114 of 117 real documents rendered, the same before and after: 82 Word files,
23 decks, 6 workbooks, 5 zips and 1 EPUB. The other three, a deck and two
zips, exceed the 100 MB expansion limit both times. No page changed. No real
file had two lists of one kind side by side that reached markdownify as two:
in Word, mammoth had already joined them (P31). Conversion took, before and
after, 12.47 s and 15.56 s for the Word files, 4.21 s and 2.99 s for the decks,
35.45 s and 46.60 s for the workbooks, 21.48 s and 28.21 s for the zips, and
0.55 s and 0.57 s for the EPUB. Those totals were taken one after the other on
a machine with a load average above 500. Timed in alternation, three runs
each, the slowest zip took 29.25 s and 31.34 s, then 34.87 s and 32.57 s, and
two workbooks 6.38 s and 5.98 s and 6.41 s and 6.50 s. Resolving that zip's
7 MB of Markdown takes 6 ms.

### P32-5: what this does not cover

- **Nested lists.** markdownify indents a list nested in an item by its
  bullet's width, 2 or 3 spaces, and Python-Markdown nests only at 4, so a
  nested list under `* ` or `1. ` to `9. ` is flattened into its parent, or
  written into the item as text. Two lists nested in one item are joined
  without even a blank line. Neither is changed here.
- **Word lists mammoth joins.** mammoth writes one `<ol>` for adjacent Word
  lists of one kind whatever their `numId`, and drops an empty paragraph
  between them, so they never reach markdownify as two. Splitting them is
  P31's; the lists it splits rely on this change to stay apart.
- **A list's start number.** nh3 drops `ol[start]` until P30, so the fixture's
  first list is numbered from 1 on the page and in `content.md`.
- **An empty item.** markdownify writes `<li></li>` as nothing, so a list
  holding only that disappears, and the lists either side of it meet.
- **A comment where none was needed.** A list in a quotation followed by one
  outside it gets the comment; Markdown kept them apart already, and the page
  is the same.

### P32-6: the tests

`tests/test_adjacent_lists.py` renders each merging case in P32-1, mammoth's
two `<ol>`s among them, and requires one list per list, no item wrapped in a
paragraph, and the same visible text as upstream's Markdown; it requires the
cases that never merged to be written exactly as upstream writes them. It
checks that a document's own private-use characters are kept, that no mark is
left in any office fixture's Markdown, that the fixture's lists come apart
across its two chapters and inside a zip, which reader resolves what, and that
a `.md` file's two lists are still one. `tests/test_office_formats.py`
captures the fixture end to end and reads `content.md`: each list a run of
its own, each numbered list after the first counting from 1, no item loose in
`content.html`, and no comment in any artifact. With the separator disabled,
43 of the 56 unit tests and the end-to-end test fail.

## P33: a zip member WebShot could not read was left out without a word (2026-10-11)

P29-5 recorded that a member nothing reads, or whose reader fails, was still
left out of the page with no warning: MarkItDown's zip reader catches both
failures and moves on, and P28's copy of it kept that. CLAUDE.md's "no silent
degradation" says otherwise. Measured on P29's change applied to P28's branch
at 9be76d6, before either merged, with MarkItDown 0.1.8, once with the CI
extras (`office` among them) and once with the base install. The fixture is
`left_out_archive.zip` in `tests/fixtures/office/`, written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`.

### P33-1: which members were left out, and why

Over 5 real zips (2,921 members) and synthetic cases:

| Member | What the zip reader met | Before | Real zips |
|---|---|---|---|
| A directory entry | `UnsupportedFormatException` (no bytes) | left out | 226 |
| An AppleDouble file (`._name`, header `00 05 16 07`) | read as text when MarkItDown took it for text, else nothing reads it | 570 in the page, 749 left out | 1,319 in 2 zips |
| A format nothing reads (`.pyc`, `.so`, `.nib`, `.tiff`, binaries with no suffix) | `UnsupportedFormatException` | left out | 590 |
| A PDF, `.xls` or Outlook `.msg` | MarkItDown's reader, missing a package no WebShot extra installs | left out | 0 |
| A deck, Word file or workbook without the office extra | MarkItDown's reader, missing its package | left out | 0 |
| A member whose reader fails | `FileConversionException`: `UnicodeDecodeError`, `BadZipFile` | left out | 1 |
| An encrypted member | `RuntimeError` from `ZipFile.read` | the whole zip fails, exit 2 | 0 |
| A damaged member (bad CRC) | `BadZipFile` from `ZipFile.read` | the whole zip fails, exit 2 | 0 |
| A CSV with a cell past the CSV reader's limit | `csv.Error`, raised as `UsageError` | the whole zip fails, exit 2 | 0 |

The real zips held no Office file, PDF, `.xls`, `.msg`, encrypted or damaged
member, so those rows are from synthetic members, and the two installs read
the real zips identically. A missing package was worse than silent: the
exception MarkItDown records carries `pip install 'markitdown[pdf]'`, advice
a WebShot user cannot follow (`_needs_a_dependency` exists to keep it from a
file on its own), and a PDF in a zip is left out on every WebShot install.

The 570 AppleDouble members in the page came from two zips the Finder made.
Each was a `## File: __MACOSX/…/._name` section of binary read as text: 160,365
characters, 2.3% of one page, and 1,928, 3.1% of the other. Of the 570, 569
carried their file's `com.apple.provenance` attribute, 6 its quarantine record
(which names the app that downloaded it), and 5 its `kMDItemWhereFroms`, the
address macOS records a downloaded file came from, which reached the page
each time. In these zips it was a site's root address; the field holds
whatever address the downloading app recorded.

### P33-2: what each gets now

Every member is in the page or named in the manifest's warnings, except a
directory entry, which holds no bytes: the files under it are members of their
own, so naming it says nothing.

- **One warning for each reason many members share.** Members nothing reads
  are one warning, naming the first three, counting the rest and tallying them
  by suffix: `572 members are not in the page: <three names> and 569 more (543
  .pyc, 16 .typed, 6 .exe, 5 with no suffix, 1 .13, 1 .so). WebShot has no
  reader for them.` One per member would have been 572 lines from a zipped
  virtualenv, burying the one that mattered.
- **A missing package gets WebShot's advice, never MarkItDown's.** A deck, a
  Word file or a workbook names `webshot[office]` in the words a file on its
  own gets, which `_dependency_advice` now holds for both. A PDF, `.xls` or
  `.msg` is counted with the members nothing reads, because no WebShot extra
  installs its reader.
- **A reason of its own is a warning of its own:** a reader that failed, with
  each error it raised and without MarkItDown's framing (`its reader failed
  (BadZipFile: File is not a zip file)`); an encrypted member, told from the
  member's flag before it is read; a member that cannot be extracted; and a
  member WebShot refuses, P29-3's `ooxml` refusal now joined by the CSV
  reader's.
- **An AppleDouble member is left out before any reader sees it**, and the
  archive gets one warning counting them. It is not a file of the archive:
  `ditto`, macOS's own unzip, turns each back into its file's extended
  attributes rather than extracting it (checked on the fixture). It is
  recognised by its name and its four-byte header together, so `._notes.txt`
  holding text is still read.

On the real zips, each page is P29's with exactly the AppleDouble sections
gone (566 and 4), byte for byte otherwise, and the download address no longer
appears in them. The zipped virtualenv now has 3 warnings, the macOS app 1 (18
members), the zip of code files 1 (5 AppleDouble members), and the zipped web
page none. The virtualenv read in 13.2 s rather than 28.2 s, since its 1,314
AppleDouble members no longer reach MarkItDown; the others took as long as
before (one run each).

### P33-3: what this does not cover

- A member read to nothing is in the page as a heading with nothing under it:
  an image or a sound, whose MarkItDown readers return only what `exiftool`
  reports, on a machine without `exiftool`; an empty file. It is named, but
  the page does not say why it is empty.
- `.DS_Store` and `Thumbs.db` are not AppleDouble. One nothing reads is named
  with the rest; one MarkItDown takes for text would be in the page.
- MarkItDown guesses a text file's encoding from its first 64 KB, so a UTF-8
  file whose first non-ASCII byte comes later is decoded as ASCII and fails:
  the virtualenv's `__init__.py` above, now named, and a CSV with its first
  `é` at byte 80,007, which on its own ends the run with exit 2.
- A zip whose every member is left out is still a capture with exit 0: a page
  with only its heading, and the warnings.

### P33-4: the tests

`tests/test_archive_members.py` holds `left_out_archive.zip`'s exact
warnings with the office extra and without it (MarkItDown's own readers, told
their packages are missing), and checks that no warning says `pip install`,
that the download address one of its AppleDouble members holds (asserted to
be there first) and its quarantine record stay off the page, that a `._` name
without the header is read, that six members nothing reads are one warning,
that a damaged member and an oversized CSV cost their member and not the
archive, that a zip inside a zip names its own, and that the warnings reach
`materialize_source`. Against P29's bridge, 8 of its 9 tests fail.
`tests/test_office_formats.py` captures the fixture end to end, finds its
four warnings in the manifest as the bridge words them, and finds the download
address in none of `content.md`, `content.txt` and `chunks.jsonl`. macOS's own
`ditto` restores the fixture's AppleDouble attributes onto its file, so the
fixture is the format the Finder writes, not one WebShot alone can read.

## P34: the lazy-load pass counted steps a page had not rendered (2026-10-11)

`tests/test_endless_feed.py::test_growth_where_exclude_removes_ends_the_pass_too`
failed once in a full `tools/verify.py` while another worktree's run shared
the Mac. It passed in isolation, three times out of three:

```
AssertionError: LazyLoadPass(steps=5, ended='bottom', height=1968, growing=(), steady_steps=0)
```

1,968 px is the page as it loads, before anything has grown. The same day a
CI run on macOS (Python 3.12, PR #179) failed in the shadow-root case of the
clean-mode test, at the same rule: `steps=4, ended='bottom', height=1545`.
Master was da7f3f8.

### P34-1: reproducing it

The probe ran the pass over the P23-8 fixture and logged the page's `scroll`
events, its IntersectionObserver callbacks and its timers. Three tries did not
reproduce it: renderer CPU throttled 8x and 20x (DevTools'
`Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate`), sixteen workers in parallel, and eight
workers beside 40 busy loops, 104 runs in all. Each of those probes also ran a
`requestAnimationFrame` loop to time frames, and in the 96 runs that timed
them the largest gap between two frames was 19 ms. With that loop taken out, the
sixteen-worker load reproduced the failure in 1 run in 64, and later in 11 in
128. The Mac's load average was 400 to 490 on 16 cores, most of it other
sessions' work. Why a page that asks for frames from the start gets its first
one sooner was not established. The loop's effect on the result was measured;
its mechanism was not. CPU throttling was then run again with no loop: 1x,
4x, 10x and 20x, over the module's four cases, six runs each. The old pass
failed none of 96 and the new pass none of 96, so a slow renderer alone does
not cause it. A late first frame does.

### P34-2: what the failing runs had in common

Each of the 11 failing runs had no first paint (`performance` `paint`
entries) and no IntersectionObserver callback at all when the pass ended, at
its fifth step about 1.0 s after it began. In the median run the observer's
first callback came before the pass's first step, and first paint came 11 ms
after `load`. The failing pass's own log shows the window at
0, 800 and then 968 px, the bottom of a 1,968 px page, and the height never
moved. Thirty-one of the 128 runs had not rendered 200 ms after the pass
began (no observer callback yet). The 20 that passed rendered 245 to 887 ms
in. The other 11 had not rendered by the end.

The pass treats a step as a chance for the page to answer a scroll. Its
original rule ends it at the bottom once the height has held for three steps,
about 0.75 s at the default `--scroll-delay`. A page sees a scroll only in a
rendering update, because Chromium fires `scroll` events there and computes
what each IntersectionObserver sees there. Those two are how pages load lazy
content, and they are how the fixture loads its feed and its list. So a page
that had not rendered could not grow, and steps that measured it were not
evidence that it had finished: a check whose input was missing (a page that
had not seen the scroll) read as success (a page that had ended). The fixture
is not at fault: it loads its
content the way pages do. Nothing in it or in the pass depends on the 600 ms
"fetch" here; every failing run ended before the first fetch could start.

A capture runs the same pass. It navigates to `domcontentloaded` and sleeps
for `--delay` (1 s by default), so a renderer whose first frame is later than
that would have its pass end at the top of an unscrolled page, with no
warning. That was not measured on a live page.

### P34-3: each step now waits for the page to render

After each scroll the pass waits for the page's next rendering update (a
`requestAnimationFrame` callback, which runs after that update's `scroll`
events), and only then starts `--scroll-delay`. If no frame comes within 30 s,
the pass stops with `ended="unrendered"` and the manifest says so
(`lazy_load_warning`). A page that never renders is not left to wait 30 s at
each of 100 steps, and a pass that saw no scroll does not read as a page that
ended.

Measured as an interleaved A/B on the same machine at the same time: sixteen
workers, each alternating the old and new pass over all four of the module's
cases (`#light` under `--exclude` and clean mode, `#shadow`, `#still`), 256
runs of each:

| Pass | Failed | `--exclude` | clean | shadow root | still |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| old | 19 of 256 | 2 of 64 | 8 of 64 | 6 of 64 | 3 of 64 |
| waits for a frame | 0 of 256 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Each old failure ended at the bottom at its fourth or fifth step, with 20 of
the 80 related logs, so all three browser tests that scroll this fixture were
exposed. On the new pass the first step's wait was a median 12 ms, 552 ms at
the 90th percentile, 2.4 s at the 99th and 3.4 s at most, with the load
average between 520 and 680. Later steps waited 4 to 13 ms (each run's
median). That frame per step is what the change costs a pass that renders
normally. The test module itself, eight copies at a time three times over at
a load average near 550, passed 24 runs of 24.

### P34-4: the boundary, and the cost on real pages

These were measured in a parallel session, interleaving the old and new pass
in one process at a load average of 490 to 560, with no
`requestAnimationFrame` instrumentation. Each was opened the way a capture
opens a page: `domcontentloaded`, then a 1 s `--delay`, then the pass at
0.25 s. The raw runs were rechecked here.

`tests/fixtures/lazy_images.html` has the same race. Its first frame was held
6 s, longer than the old pass takes (about 4.5 s), by a render-blocking script
served late. The old pass still ended "at the bottom" in 18 steps, and
`below.png` was not requested during it in 4 runs of 4 at 1x and 10x CPU
throttling. At 20x it was requested in 2 of 4, because the slower pass
outlasted the hold. On the new pass it was requested in 4 of 4 at every rate,
in 9.5 to 10.2 s against 4.5 to 5.4 s unheld; the difference is the held
frame. In all 48 runs the capture's `_wait_for_fonts_and_images` still had
`below.png` loaded before print. Its eager switch rescues an image marked
`loading="lazy"`, but it cannot rescue content a script loads when an
IntersectionObserver fires, such as the fixture's related list.

On three real pages, clean mode, four runs of each pass, both passes ended at
the bottom in the same number of steps:

| Page | Steps | Median wall, old → new |
|---|---|---|
| en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse | 19 | 4.77 → 4.95 s |
| developer.mozilla.org, Intersection Observer API | 28 | 21.03 → 21.40 s |
| github.com/microsoft/playwright | 13 | 9.34 → 9.59 s |

That is 9 to 20 ms per step. On the fixture the median pass grew 0.03 to
0.40 s, with the same step count or one or two fewer. This table predates
P34-5, which changes how MDN and GitHub scroll.

### P34-5: a page that scrolls smoothly hung the pass

In Chromium 153 (153.0.8010.12, Playwright 1.63), `window.scrollBy` and
`window.scrollTo` return a promise that settles when the scroll has finished,
and `page.evaluate` waits for a promise it is handed. On a page with
`html { scroll-behavior: smooth }` the scroll animates, so every step waited
for the animation. On such a page that is not rendering, the animation never
runs and the promise never settles. The pass then hung in its scroll call,
before the frame wait could time out. P37 ran master f2be8dd the same way.
Held, the smooth page had no result after 20 s, and the plain page ended
`bottom` at step 5.

The session measuring the pass's per-step cost (P37) found this, and it was
reproduced here. `#late-frame` was held for ever with the frame wait cut to
1.5 s. The plain page ended `unrendered` in 1.52 s. The same page scrolling
smoothly had no result after 20 s.

Both scrolls are now `instant`, and the function that makes them hands
nothing back, so the only wait in a step is the frame wait, which has a bound.
With both changed, the smooth page ends `unrendered` in 1.53 s. With only the
step's scroll changed, P37 found the pass hung in its last scroll back to the
top. On the smooth fixture with nothing held, three interleaved runs of each:

| Scroll | Per step | Steps | Pass |
|---|---|---|---|
| old | 0.79–1.01 s | 15 | 11.9–15.1 s |
| `instant` | 0.26 s | 19 | 4.9–5.0 s |

Every run ended at `removed-growth` with all 80 related logs. The old scroll
needed fewer steps because each one lasted longer, and the patience counts
seconds as well as steps. MDN and github.com/microsoft/playwright both scroll
smoothly. There, P37 measured the scroll call at 492 ms a step, against
0.7 ms on Wikipedia, which is the whole of their 0.7 s steps in P34-4's
table. Measuring the page's state took about 5 ms a step.

### P34-6: the tests

`#late-frame` in `tests/fixtures/endless_feed.html` adds a render-blocking
script (`blocking="render"`) that a test serves when it chooses. The test
serves the fixture through `page.route` from a `.test` origin and navigates to
`domcontentloaded`, as a capture does. The page then cannot render until the
script arrives. Held 2 s, the old pass fails with the reported assertion,
`steps=5, ended='bottom', height=1968`, three times out of three with no
added load, and the new pass reaches `removed-growth` with all 80 related logs.
Held until the pass ends, with the frame wait cut to 1.5 s, the pass stops
after one step as `unrendered` and its warning says so. A unit test pins the
warning's text. Opened from disk, the script is missing and its load fails at
once, so every other variant renders as before. `#late-frame-smooth` adds
`scroll-behavior: smooth`, and both late-frame tests run on it too. The tests
give the pass 60 s, so a hang fails rather than stalling the run. With the
old scroll calls put back, the smooth `unrendered` case fails that way.

## P37: the lazy-load pass's slow steps were smooth scrolling, not its measurement (2026-10-11)

P34-4 timed the pass on three real pages at the default 0.25 s
`--scroll-delay`. A step took about 0.75 s on developer.mozilla.org and
github.com, and 0.25 s on Wikipedia. The suspect for the extra half second was
`LAZY_LOAD_STATE_JS` (P23-8). When the capture removes anything (clean mode's
`NOISE_SELECTORS`, or `--exclude`), that script matches the removed regions,
walks every element outside them and into open shadow roots, reads a box for
each leaf, and sizes each region. Faithful mode without `--exclude` skips all
of it. The suspect was the wrong one. The script costs about 5 ms a step on
those pages. The half second is the scroll call waiting for the page's
smooth-scroll animation.

### P37-1: how it was measured

A script replayed the pass as P34-3 left it (measure, scroll, wait for a
frame, `--scroll-delay`), with the module's own rules for ending it, and timed
each call separately:

- a `() => 0` round trip, the floor for any call into the page;
- the state script's round trip, and inside it, by `performance.now()`, the
  selector match, the walk with its box reads, and the region sizing;
- the scroll call and the frame wait.

Each page was opened as a capture opens it: `DEFAULT_VIEWPORT`,
`domcontentloaded`, 1 s, then the pass at 0.25 s. Each page ran four times in
clean mode and four in faithful mode, alternating which went first, in
headless Chromium 153.0.8010.12 under Playwright 1.63. No
`requestAnimationFrame` loop was added; the pass's own frame wait was the only
one. A fifth run read the renderer main thread's CPU time (`ThreadTime`, from
DevTools' `Performance.getMetrics`) around each state call.

The Mac's load average stayed between 118 and 353 throughout, most of it other
sessions' work, and no quieter window came. Neither finding depends on it. The
state script's time inside the page matched its main-thread CPU time to within
1 ms a call (58.2 ms against 58.7 ms at YouTube's step 47), so load did not
stretch it. And the scroll's half second is an animation of fixed length.

### P37-2: what each part of a step costs

Medians per step in clean mode, in milliseconds. "Script" is the state
script's round trip. "Match" and "walk" are its parts timed inside the page,
and the walk includes its box reads and the timers around them. The kept count
includes open shadow roots, which is why MDN's is larger than the 1,049
elements in its document.

| Page | Steps | Kept | Script | Match | Walk | Scroll call | Frame wait |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| developer.mozilla.org, Intersection Observer API | 28 | 5,366 | 5.7 | 0.3 | 4.0 | 492 | 16 |
| github.com/microsoft/playwright | 13 | 2,325 | 5.9 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 492 | 16 |
| en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse | 19 | 2,316 | 4.8 | 1.3 | 1.7 | 1.0 | 9 |
| en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II | 64–65 | 13,733 | 17.1 | 4.9 | 10.0 | 1.1 | 13 |
| a YouTube watch page | 33–59 | 16,359 | 42.7 | 29.8 | 6.6 | 1.5 | 17 |

In faithful mode the script's round trip was 1.0–1.7 ms, no more than the
`() => 0` floor (1.2–1.6 ms). The scroll call and the frame wait were the same
as in clean mode.

Whole passes say the same. On MDN, github.com and Lighthouse, 9 of the 12
clean and faithful pairs took the same time to within 0.5 s, with clean as
often faster as slower. The other three were faithful passes, slower by 1.7 s,
5.6 s and 33 s, most of it in their scroll calls. On World War II, clean took
0.9–3.1 s longer than faithful in all four pairs. Its script added up to
1.0–1.3 s a pass, and the rest of the gap was not attributed. On YouTube,
clean passes ended at `removed-growth` after 33–59 steps in 11.2–22.5 s, with
the script 10–16% of each pass. Three faithful passes ran to the 100-step
limit in 30.9–34.0 s, and one was served a page that ended after 6 steps.

### P37-3: the half second is the page's smooth scrolling

In this Chromium, `window.scrollBy` returns a Promise that settles when the
scroll has finished, and `page.evaluate` waits for a Promise its expression
returns. MDN and github.com set `html { scroll-behavior: smooth }`. Each
step's scroll therefore animated, and the call came back about 500 ms later,
in clean and faithful mode alike. Wikipedia's `scroll-behavior` is `auto`,
and the call came back in 0.6–2.3 ms, each pass's median. On MDN and
github.com, `void window.scrollBy(...)` and `behavior: 'instant'` both came
back in under 1 ms. The animation is the whole difference between those pages' steps of
0.61–0.75 s and Wikipedia's of 0.25–0.29 s, and it is in P34-4's figures for
both the old pass and the new.

The same Promise hung the pass on a page that does not render. With a page's
first frame held behind a render-blocking script, a smooth `scrollBy` came back
3.50 s after a 3 s hold and 10.50 s after a 10 s hold. With `auto` it came
back in 0.01 s either way. On #182 at 3931f5c, with the frame wait cut to
1.5 s and `#late-frame` held for ever, the pass ended `unrendered` after
1.5 s. With `html { scroll-behavior: smooth; }` added to the fixture, it had
not returned after 20 s, when the probe cancelled it. The 30 s guard could not
fire, because the call that waited was the scroll and not the frame wait.
Making only the step's scroll `instant` moved the hang to the final
`window.scrollTo(0, 0)`. With both `instant`, the smooth page ended
`unrendered` in 1.5 s like the plain one. On master at f2be8dd, which has no
frame wait, the held smooth page had not returned after 20 s either, and the
held plain page ended `bottom` at step 5, P34's failure. The print CSS sets
`html { scroll-behavior: auto !important; }`, but only after the pass. P34-5
makes both scrolls instant and adds a smooth variant of the fixture.

### P37-4: where the state script does cost something

On the YouTube page the script grows with the page, and what grows is the
match, not the walk. One clean pass, in milliseconds:

| Step | Elements in the document | In removed regions | Kept | Script | Match | Walk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4,435 | 122 | 3,516 | 6.6 | 3.2 | 2.9 |
| 31 | 50,439 | 38,147 | 11,495 | 52.9 | 43.4 | 8.3 |
| 59 | 87,716 | 70,560 | 16,359 | 96.2 | 80.1 | 12.6 |

The match is a `document.querySelectorAll` per selector list, about 0.9 µs
for each element in the document. By the end most of the document is inside
the comment feed, which the walk never enters but the match still searches.
Matching during the walk instead, with `Element.matches` on each light-tree
element the walk reaches, would test the 16,359 kept elements and the regions'
roots rather than 87,716 elements. It was not built. Its saving is at most the
match's median 30 ms of a 340–440 ms step, on the largest page measured. And
the pass has to decide exactly as before, so the new match would have to
reproduce what `document.querySelectorAll` does and does not see: shadow trees
it does not search, a match on `html` or `body`, and the selector-by-selector
fallback for an invalid `--exclude`.

The pass is not changed here. The walk is not the cost on any page measured,
and the smooth-scroll hang is fixed where the frame wait is, in P34-5.
## P36: a converted document's pictures were not its own (2026-10-11)

A deck with one picture was captured with no picture in it, one failed
`file:` request, and the generic warning "1 request for the page's resources
failed". MarkItDown 0.1.8 reads decks with python-pptx 1.0.2 and Word files
with mammoth 1.11.0. Master was f2be8dd. The fixtures are `picture_deck.pptx`,
`picture_report.docx` and `picture_book.epub` in `tests/fixtures/office/`,
written by `tools/fixtures/office.py`.

### P36-1: what each reader did with a picture

| Format | What MarkItDown wrote | What the capture did |
|---|---|---|
| `.pptx` | `![alt](Picture2.jpg)`, a name made from the shape's | requested `Picture2.jpg` in the deck's folder |
| `.docx` | `![alt](data:image/png;base64...)`, cut short | drew a broken image, with no request and no warning |
| `.epub` | the chapter's own path, `images/blue.png` | requested it in the book's folder |
| `.xlsx` | nothing: MarkItDown writes no picture unless asked | unchanged |

The page's base is the document's folder, so a name or a path resolved there.
With nothing of that name it failed. With something of that name it worked:
a red PNG called `Picture2.jpg` beside the deck became the slide's picture,
under the deck's own alt text, and the capture said nothing. Two pictures in a
deck can be given the same name, so both took the same file. A picture that
failed to load still became a visual asset, a screenshot of the broken frame
around its alt text, 140 by 26 pixels, sent to OCR like any picture.

### P36-2: each picture is its own bytes, or a line saying why not

- MarkItDown's `keep_data_uris` option makes a deck's picture a `data:` URL
  of its own bytes, and keeps mammoth's `data:` URL whole.
- An EPUB chapter's path is read from inside the book, resolved against the
  chapter's own path there, and becomes a `data:` URL.
- Chromium draws PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, SVG, AVIF and icons. A TIFF is
  written again as PNG through Pillow. A WMF, an EMF or a JPEG XR is drawn by
  nothing WebShot ships, so it becomes a line of text in the page, `[Picture:
  alt — not shown: a Windows Metafile (WMF), which a browser cannot draw]`,
  and a warning naming its slide.
- A deck picture with no bytes, which the deck only links to, gets the same
  treatment.
- A converted page never names a picture by a path for the browser to
  resolve: a path the reader cannot read becomes text and a warning. A remote
  picture is the document's own and is fetched, as an HTML file's is.
- MarkItDown's Markdown for a picture is read strictly. A release that writes
  it differently raises an error rather than putting an unchecked URL in the page.
- `img` is held to the page's width, since a slide's photograph is often
  wider than the column.

Recording each `data:` URL verbatim then put the pictures into `assets.json`
as base64: 5 MB for one deck of 26 pictures. When the capture keeps its source
file under `source/`, the bytes are already in the bundle. So `assets.json`
records such a URL by its type and length:
`data:image/png;base64,… (123,456 characters; the picture is in source/)`.
A web page's `data:` URL holds the only copy of its picture as the page had
it, and is recorded whole, as before.

### P36-3: real files

Over 178 real files (23 decks, 81 Word files, 6 workbooks, 1 EPUB, 5 zips, 62
CSVs), the page body of 138 was byte-identical. The other 40 differed in their
pictures alone: 301 pictures drawn (220 PNG, 74 JPEG, 7 GIF) where none had
been. Five decks hold 26 WMF pictures, the clip art of older Office versions,
and one holds a TIFF. A zipped web page names its two pictures by path. These
are now warnings, and the TIFF is drawn. Conversion took 2.94 s before and
11.46 s after for the decks, 13.58 s and 17.10 s for the Word files, and 0.73 s
and 1.34 s for the EPUB. The rest were level. For the largest deck, 0.56 s of
4.1 s is Python-Markdown's link parser reading each picture's URL a character
at a time.

Three decks captured end to end:
- The one with 26 pictures went from a 512 KB PDF with 5 failed requests to a
  4.0 MB PDF with every picture in it and none failed. Its `assets.json` went
  from 20 KB to 17 KB.
- The one with 17 WMF pictures went from 17 broken-frame assets and 8 failed
  requests to no assets, none failed, and 17 warnings, one per slide.
- The one with the TIFF went from 11 failed requests to none, with the TIFF
  drawn.

### P36-4: what this does not cover

- A WMF or EMF picture is named, not drawn: no renderer here reads one.
- A picture an HTML file in a zip names by path is not read from the zip; it
  is a line of text. The real case is a web page saved with its pictures.
- A `.md` file is Markdown, in a zip or not, and a picture it names by path
  still resolves beside it.
- A picture is drawn whole: a crop set on the slide (`a:srcRect`) is not
  applied, and nor is the size it was given there.
- MarkItDown writes no picture from a workbook.

### P36-5: the tests

`tests/test_office_pictures.py` covers:
- which formats pass as they are, and the TIFF written again as PNG with its
  pixels;
- each format refused, with its reason, and a path never left for the browser;
- each fixture's pictures, placeholders and warnings, with the deck read
  beside a file for every name MarkItDown makes up;
- alt text in a placeholder, encoded once all the way to the page;
- `assets.json`'s record of a kept file's `data:` URL against a web page's.

`tests/test_office_formats.py` captures the three fixtures end to end and
checks:
- no request failed;
- the warnings in the manifest;
- the visual assets, by alt text;
- each asset's recorded source, by type and length.

Two P28 tests expected mammoth's cut-short URL, and now find the picture whole.
The HTML converter's parity test now names its picture remotely, since a path
is a placeholder here and a picture upstream.
## P39: a page that scrolls smoothly printed its boxes partway back (2026-10-11)

The visual harvest saves every scroll position before its first screenshot and
puts each one back when it is done, because Chromium prints a scrolling box and
a frame as they stand (P16-9, P16-12). It put them back with `scrollTo(x, y)`
and `scrollTop =`, and both obey the page's `scroll-behavior`. On a page that
sets `smooth` they start an animation and return. MDN and github.com set it on
`html` (P37-3, in the entry on the lazy-load pass's step cost). The report that opened this measured a window at 1,500 px and
a box at 900 px: both still there when the restore returned, with no failure
counted, 1,417 and 797 at 100 ms, and 0 at 1 s.

Measured with Chromium 153.0.8010.12 and Playwright 1.63 on macOS. The fixture
is `smooth_scrolled_visuals_page.html`: P16-12's `scrolled_visuals_page.html`
with `scroll-behavior: smooth` on the window, on each box and on the capped
frame. Scroll positions were read with `page.evaluate` alone. No
`requestAnimationFrame` loop went into the page, because one changes when it
renders (P34).

### P39-1: what a print during the animation shows

The shadow box and the capped frame were scrolled to their end with
`behavior: 'instant'`, as the harvest's screenshots leave them, and the window
to 764 px. Then came the restore, a wait, and `page.pdf()`:

| Print after the restore | Box and frame at the print | Each one printed |
|---|---|---|
| 0 ms, twice | 563 px | its bottom sentence |
| 50 ms | 552 px | its bottom sentence |
| 100 ms | 426 px | neither sentence |
| 200 ms | 95 px | neither sentence |
| 400 ms | 0 | its top sentence |
| 800 ms, 1.5 s | 0 | its top sentence |

The restore counted no failure in any row. Printing does not stop the
animation: across the 100 ms row's print the box went on from 426 to 327 px.
The window, 764 px away, still had 8 px to go at 400 ms.

### P39-2: when a capture prints

A full capture was run with `capture_visual_assets`, `extract_semantic_content`
and `Page.pdf` wrapped to read the positions as each was reached. The harvest
left the shadow box and the frame at their end, 518 px, and the window at 0.

- **The snapshot** starts 1 to 2 ms after the restore, with both at 518 px. It
  is not affected: of an element's geometry it reads only whether its box has
  a width and a height (`VISIBLE_JS` and `rendered`), and scrolling changes
  neither.
- **The print, in the first capture in a process**, came 2.8 to 12.6 s after
  the restore, because the extraction between them pays docling's start-up.
  The animation had ended, and the PDF was right.
- **The print, from the second capture on**, came 62, 79 and 82 ms after the
  restore, in three captures in one process, with both at 448 to 488 px. The
  clipping check's print followed at 106 to 149 ms, with both at 162 to 280
  px. The PDF printed neither of the shadow box's sentences nor either of the
  capped frame's, and no warning said so.

The MCP server runs each capture inside its own long-running process, so every
capture after its first is the second case. A single CLI capture was safe only
because docling took longer to start than the animation took to finish. That
depends on how fast the machine is.

### P39-3: put back at once, and read back

`RESTORE_SCROLL_JS` now scrolls with `behavior: 'instant'`: `scrollTo({left,
top, behavior})` on a window and on an element alike. It still returns a
count, never the promise Chromium 153's scroll methods return, so `evaluate`
waits on no scroll (P34). With it, every row of P39-1 printed both top
sentences, and the restore returned with both at 0. Three captures in one
process printed them too, 61 to 108 ms after the restore.

The count rose only when something threw, and a scroll that does not take
throws nothing. That is how a restore that left every box where the harvest
had put it reported none that would not go back. Each position is now read
back after its scroll, and one that differs is counted, so the existing
warning fires. A box whose content shrank below its saved position is one. A
box or frame the page removed is skipped, because neither prints. Inside a
removed frame an element is still `isConnected`, to a document whose
`defaultView` is null, and the first version of this counted that frame's
`html`. The comparison is exact. An offset of 100.7 px in a box under
`zoom: 1.37`, which reads 100.72992706298828, read back the same at device
scale factors 1, 1.25, 2 and 3.

### P39-4: the other scrolls in `src/webshot`

- **Playwright's scroll into view before a screenshot** is instant. On the
  smooth page the harvest's last screenshot had left both boxes at their end,
  518 px, by the time it returned.
- **The lazy-load pass** scrolls with `window.scrollBy` and
  `window.scrollTo(0, 0)`. P34-5 (#182) makes both instant.
- **The protected viewer's `set_scroll`** sets `scrollTop` and waits 500 ms
  before each segment's screenshot. Its jumps are a page apart, and a 764 px
  smooth scroll was still moving at 400 ms, so if SharePoint's viewer scrolls
  smoothly a segment could be taken short of where it is clipped. Nothing here
  says whether it does. `tests/fixtures/viewer/dom/` records the viewer's
  accessibility tree, not its CSS, and no test drives the segmented capture in
  a browser. So it is left as it is, and noted as follow-up work.
- Nothing else scrolls: `scrollTo`, `scrollBy`, `scrollTop =`, `scrollLeft =`,
  `scrollIntoView` and `mouse.wheel` appear nowhere else.

### P39-5: the tests

In `tests/test_shadow_frame_visuals.py`, all three fail without the change:

- `test_the_harvest_puts_back_every_scroll_position_it_moved` runs on both
  pages. Before, on the smooth one, the boxes were still at the harvest's
  positions when it returned.
- `test_a_position_that_did_not_go_back_is_counted`: a box whose content
  shrinks below its position counts, and a removed box and a removed frame do
  not. Before, the count was 0.
- `test_a_smoothly_scrolling_box_prints_from_where_the_page_had_it` captures the
  smooth page twice in one process. Before, the second capture printed neither
  of the shadow box's sentences.
## P42: a smoothly scrolling viewer had its first segment shot mid-scroll (2026-10-11)

P39-4 left one scroll in `src/webshot` as it was: the protected viewer's
`set_scroll`. It set the viewer's `scrollTop`, dispatched a `scroll` event,
waited 500 ms, and the segment's screenshot was then clipped as if the viewer
stood at the target. `scrollTop =` obeys `scroll-behavior`. Nothing recorded
whether SharePoint's viewer scrolls smoothly, because
`tests/fixtures/viewer/dom/` holds its accessibility tree and not its CSS, and
no test drove the segmented capture in a browser.

Measured with Chromium 153.0.8010.12 and Playwright 1.63 on macOS, at the
capture's own geometry: a 1440 × 1000 window at device scale factor 2. The
fixtures are `sharepoint-portrait.html`, whose three pages now draw eleven
96 px colour bands each, no two alike, and `sharepoint-portrait-smooth.html`,
the same page with `scroll-behavior: smooth` on the viewer container. Its
viewer is 820 px tall, and its pages 1,056 px with 24 px between them.
Positions were read with `page.evaluate` alone. No `requestAnimationFrame`
loop went into the page, because one changes when it renders (P34).

### P42-1: how long a smooth scroll of the viewer takes

Each distance was set with `scrollTop =` from the top, and the position read
back every 20 ms or so, so an arrival time is late by up to about 25 ms:

| Distance | Still to go at 400 ms | at 500 ms | Arrived |
|---|---|---|---|
| 236 px | arrived | arrived | 247 ms |
| 844 px | 6 px | arrived | 470 ms |
| 900 px | 9 px | arrived | 489 ms |
| 1,000 px | 17 px | 1 px | 547 ms |
| 1,500 px | 102 px | 30 px | 635 ms |
| 2,000 px | 225 px | 82 px | 739 ms |
| 3,000 px | 528 px | 317 px | 909 ms |

From one segment to the next, the capture scrolls either by a page's overhang
(its height less the viewer's, 236 px here) or by the viewer's height plus the
gap between pages (844 px here). The two segments of a page must overlap, so
neither is longer than about the viewer's height plus the gap. In this fixture
both landed inside the wait, the longer by about 30 ms. A viewer that filled
more of the 1,000 px window would cut that: a 1,000 px scroll was still 1 px
short at 500 ms.

The first scroll is different. It starts wherever the viewer is, which P8-45
says is wherever the reader left it, and from there it can cross the whole
document.

### P42-2: the segments the capture took

The capture ran on each fixture from the top and from the last page, with
`scrollTop` read just before each screenshot:

- **The plain fixture**, from either start: every segment at its target.
- **The smooth fixture, from the top**: every segment at its target. The
  scrolls were 24, 236 and 844 px.
- **The smooth fixture, from the last page**: the first scroll is 2,444 px,
  from 2,468 to 24. Just before page 1's top segment was shot the viewer read
  205 or 229 px, and the next scroll found it at 163, so the shot came while
  it moved. In five runs of the test below, page 1's stitched upper half was
  89 to 159 px out of place. Every later segment was at its target, because
  each later scroll started from where the first had got to. The capture
  reported nothing.
- **The synthetic `scroll` event** fired before the box had moved, every time
  the viewer scrolled smoothly: `scrollTop` read straight after the call still
  held the old position.

### P42-3: scroll at once, and read it back

`set_scroll` now calls `viewer.scrollTo({top, behavior: 'instant'})`, so the
viewer is at the target, and dispatches the synthetic event after the move.
The function hands back nothing, because Chromium 153's `scrollTo` returns a
promise that `page.evaluate` would wait on (P34-5).

`scroll_to_segment` then reads `scrollTop` back after the 500 ms wait, as the
screenshot will find it, and raises with both positions when it is more than
half a pixel from the target. The half pixel is Chromium's rounding. The
target comes from `getBoundingClientRect`, so it can be fractional, and the
viewer keeps its offset in whole CSS pixels at device scale factors 1, 1.25, 2
and 3: 24.3 read back 24, 1104.5 read back 1105 and 2467.9 read back 2468. A
target past the end of the scroll range reads back clamped: 2,500 read back
2,468.

The scroll back to the top after the last segment is not checked. Nothing is
shot after it, and a viewer that will not sit at 0 should not cost a finished
capture. The 500 ms wait stays: it is there for the viewer to draw what the
scroll reveals, which an instant scroll does not change. With the change
every segment, on both fixtures from both starts, was shot at its target, and
a capture took about 3.4 s, as before.

### P42-4: what reading it back catches

A viewer that snaps its scroll to points inside its pages. With
`scroll-snap-type: y mandatory` on the container and `scroll-snap-align:
start` on the fixture's bands, page 1's bottom segment, asked for at 260 px,
went to the band at 216. The old code shot every bottom segment 44 px high:
each stitched page held 44 px of itself twice at the seam, as a band 280 rows
tall where it draws 192, and lost its last 44 px, and the capture reported
nothing. Now it stops: "The viewer was scrolled to 260px for a page segment
but is at 216px". Snap points on whole pages hold nothing. A snap area taller
than the viewer lets any position inside it stand, so every segment stayed
where it was put.

### P42-5: what it does not catch

Every page is shot where page 1's position and height, and the step from page
1 to page 2, say it is: page *n* at `page_top + (n - 1) * step`. In a document
whose pages differ in size, every page after the first that differs is shot
from the wrong place, and the scroll there still takes, so the read-back sees
nothing wrong. It is caught only when the error puts a segment past the end
of the scroll range, and there the capture now stops where it used to stitch
the page with its seam out of place. This is from the code, not measured.
Measuring each page before its segments are shot would fix both, and is left
as follow-up work. P46 measures it and does that.

Whether SharePoint's viewer scrolls smoothly is still unrecorded. The capture
no longer depends on it.

### P42-6: the tests

In `tests/test_protected_viewer.py`, both fail without the change:

- `test_each_stitched_page_is_its_own_page_band_for_band` runs the capture on
  both fixtures from the last page and names every row of each stitched
  page's middle column by the band it shows. Before, the smooth fixture failed
  on page 1 in five runs of five.
- `test_a_segment_the_viewer_would_not_scroll_to_is_refused` runs it on the
  snapping viewer above. Before, the capture did not raise.
## P41: a table's capture time grew with the square of its cells (2026-10-11)

P35-3 (pull request #192) recorded it: captures of a 2-column CSV took 26 s,
57 s and 179 s at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 rows, an 11,431-row one ran past 40
minutes, and a profile put 23.6 s of a 76 s capture in docling-core's DocTags
writer rebuilding `TableData.grid`. Measured here on master at 5a5a6ab with
docling-core 2.99.0, the version `uv.lock` pins, and on 2.101.1, the newest
release (2026-10-08).

### P41-1: where the grid is read

`TableData.grid` is a pydantic computed property. Every read builds the whole
grid again: a list per row, the table's own cell at each position it covers
and a new empty `TableCell` everywhere else. `TableItem.export_to_otsl`, which
`DocTagsTableSerializer` calls for each table in `export_to_doctags()`, reads
`self.data.grid[i][j]` inside its loop over rows and columns. That is one
build per cell, not per row as P35-3 has it, so a table of n cells builds n
grids and n² cells, and a table twice as wide costs four times as much too.

Counting the builds over one capture of a 250-row, 2-column CSV gave 510:
502 from `export_to_otsl` (251 rows, the header among them, times 2), and 8
that do not grow with the table: the Markdown table serializer reads it twice
and runs three times, for `content.md`, `content.txt` and the chunker, then
`export_to_dict` and the bridge's own `tables` read it once each. The 1,000-row profile's
2,010 reads are the same split: 2,002 and 8.

docling-core's DocLang writer, `DocLangTableSerializer._emit_otsl`, reads the
grid per cell the same way; WebShot does not write DocLang. docling-core fixed
this pattern in its HTML serializer (docling-project/docling-core#373) and its
DataFrame export (docling-project/docling-core#754) but not in these two, and 2.101.1 and its main branch at 0d5a7bd still read
per cell. On main, `export_to_doctags()` alone took 2.1 s, 11.9 s and 57.7 s
for a constructed 500, 1,000 and 2,000-row table of 2 columns.

### P41-2: the fix

The bridge wraps `export_to_doctags()` in `_grids_built_once`. For the
export, each table's `data` is swapped for an instance of a `TableData`
subclass whose `grid` is one grid built up front, and the original is put back
afterwards, as `_doctags` already does with code languages it cannot spell.
The copy shares the original's cells; only its `grid` differs, and the grid
is a function of the cells and the table's size, which an export does not
change. A `data` of any type but `TableData` itself is left alone, since a
copy would drop what a subclass adds. The 250-row capture now builds 9 grids,
and the count no longer depends on the table.

The output is byte for byte docling-core's. On `spanning_table.html`, whose
table has header rows spanning columns, a header spanning rows, row headers,
cells spanning rows, columns and both, empty cells, and cells holding a list,
bold text and a nested table, `extract` with and without the swap gives the
same DocTags, `content.json`, Markdown and tables. Its DocTags hold every OTSL
token but `srow`, which docling's HTML backend writes only for a
`row_section` class, an attribute the snapshot sanitizer removes. Bundles of
the 250-row CSV from master and the branch differ only in `captured_at`, the
PDF's name and its digest.

### P41-3: what it costs now

End to end, `webshot <file> --output x.pdf --no-ocr` on synthetic inputs,
master and the branch alternating, two rounds. The machine was running three
CI runners' test suites and other sessions' gauntlets at the same time (load
average 120 to 350), so single times swing widely; the 145.5 s is the branch
during the worst of it.

| Input | Master, round 1 | Branch, round 1 | Master, round 2 | Branch, round 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CSV, 500 × 2 | 14.9 s | 14.4 s | 18.0 s | 20.0 s |
| CSV, 1,000 × 2 | 42.0 s | 25.7 s | 34.3 s | 145.5 s |
| CSV, 2,000 × 2 | 83.6 s | 39.2 s | 209.7 s | 40.1 s |
| HTML `<table>`, 2,000 × 3 | 174.0 s | 28.1 s | 227.9 s | 29.6 s |

The changed step on its own: `docling_bridge.extract` run once on each
capture's `content.html` (the snapshot it was handed, identical from both
sides), master's bridge and the branch's in separate processes, with process
CPU time, which the load disturbs less than wall time.

| Input | Cells | Grid builds, master | CPU, master | Grid builds, branch | CPU, branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CSV, 500 × 2 | 1,002 | 1,010 | 3.16 s | 9 | 1.12 s |
| CSV, 1,000 × 2 | 2,002 | 2,010 | 12.65 s | 9 | 1.35 s |
| CSV, 2,000 × 2 | 4,002 | 4,010 | 58.99 s | 9 | 2.04 s |
| HTML `<table>`, 2,000 × 3 | 6,003 | 6,011 | 131.94 s | 9 | 1.77 s |

Every `ExtractionResult` field was equal between the two, and each capture's
`content.*`, `chunks.jsonl` and `tables/` were byte-identical across the two
bundles. The 1,000-row count, 2,010, is P35-3's profile's.

### P41-4: real files

Every CSV in one real folder outside vendored packages: 31 files, 14 distinct
by content, copied out and captured with the branch. For nine of them
`extract` ran on the capture's snapshot with master's bridge and the
branch's, as in P41-3. Every field was equal, and the branch built 9 grids
for each.

| Rows × columns | Cells | Grid builds, master | CPU, master | CPU, branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 35 × 2 | 70 | 78 | 0.97 s | 0.96 s |
| 26 × 3 | 78 | 86 | 0.88 s | 0.89 s |
| 11 × 11 | 121 | 129 | 0.92 s | 0.89 s |
| 7 × 33 | 231 | 239 | 0.96 s | 0.88 s |
| 151 × 5 | 755 | 763 | 2.11 s | 0.99 s |
| 261 × 8 | 2,088 | 2,096 | 11.51 s | 1.22 s |
| 261 × 10 | 2,610 | 2,618 | 18.98 s | 1.33 s |
| 681 × 7 | 4,767 | 4,775 | 73.15 s | 1.65 s |
| 1,075 × 10 | 10,750 | 10,758 | 398.09 s | 2.51 s |

Rows count the header. Master was not run on the rest, since the cost grows
with the square of the cells: two more 1,075 × 10 files, and three larger
ones. A 299 × 75 survey export (22,425 cells) took 4.38 s on the branch with
9 builds, and by the square about 29 minutes on master; its capture took 94 s
end to end. The largest, 54,832 × 3 (164,496 cells), finished its bundle,
extraction included, and reached the PDF step 661 s into the capture. There
Chromium's renderer crashed on a page 1,864,558 px tall and the run exited 7,
a long-page limit this change does not touch. By the square, master would have
spent about 26 hours of CPU building grids for it. An 875 × 85 survey export
(74,375 cells) was stopped after 24 minutes in the lazy-load pass, under the
load above, before it reached extraction.

### P41-5: the tests, and upstream

`tests/test_table_grid_builds.py` counts `TableData.grid` builds rather than
timing anything: `spanning_table.html` must build as many grids as the same
table with its last body ten times as long. With the swap turned off it fails
on the fixture alone, 65 builds against a bound of 52 (the fixture's 52
cells). It also holds the DocTags, `content.json`, Markdown and tables to the
unswapped export's, requires every OTSL token but `srow` in them, and checks
that a table gets its own `data` back when the export raises. The bridge's
tests pass on docling-core 2.101.1 as on 2.99.0.

Reported upstream as docling-project/docling-core#862, with the fix,
reading the grid once before the loop in both writers, as
docling-project/docling-core#863. Its test counts grid reads too, and fails on
main. On main, `export_to_doctags()` of a 2,000 × 2 table took 57.7 s and with
the change 0.010 s. Once a docling-core release carries it, the swap changes
nothing, since the writer then reads the grid once itself, and
`_grids_built_once` can go; the count test holds either way.
## P45: a list item that holds only a list had no line in content.md (2026-10-11)

An `<li>` with no text of its own, holding only a list, is what mammoth writes
for Word bullets at level 1 with none at level 0, and what P40's fixture
`nested_book.epub` holds under "An item that is only a list". Its content.md
was

```
    - Gorvane
    - Holvish
- Istrel
```

with no line for the outer item. Measured with docling-slim 2.132.0,
docling-core 2.99.0 and markdown-it-py 4.2.0 (a CommonMark reader) on master
5a5a6ab. The fixture is `tests/fixtures/item_holding_a_list.html`; every word
in it is made up.

### P45-1: what docling does with such an item

`HTMLDocumentBackend._handle_list` reads each `<li>`'s text with its lists left
out (`ignore_list=True`). When none is left, `_add_list_item_with_content`
makes no item, and the lists inside go to `_handle_block`, which hangs them off
the outer list's group. The counter that numbers an `<ol start>` counts only
the items made. So:

- In content.json the nested list is a child of the outer list, the shape an
  invalid `<ul><li>A</li><ul>…</ul></ul>` also gives, so nothing after the
  conversion can tell the two apart. The empty item is not there.
- docling-core's Markdown serializer writes a nested list four spaces in per
  level and an item as `marker text`. With no item there is no marker line,
  and the nested list's lines come straight after whatever preceded it.
- Without `start`, the serializer numbers an item by its position among the
  group's children, the nested group included, so the next item's number was
  right (`3.` after `1.` and the missing `2.`). With `start`, the backend's own
  marker counts only the items it made: `<ol start="5">` with the empty item
  second wrote the third as `6.`, in content.json and content.md.

Read back with a CommonMark reader, master's content.md for the fixture:

| The empty item | master's content.md | Read as |
|---|---|---|
| first, after a paragraph | `    - Gorvane` | a code block |
| first of a list under an item with text | `        - Kelmar` | the parent's text: `Jaskov - Kelmar - Lunden` |
| two levels of them | `        - Nalder` | a code block |
| second of a numbered list | `1. Quenby`, `    1. Raskel`, `3. Tallow` | Raskel under Quenby |
| second of `<ol start="5">` | `5. Umber`, `    - Varrick`, `6. Wendle` | Varrick under Umber, Wendle 6, not 7 |
| holding a `<ul>` and an `<ol>` | `    - Yarrow`, `    1. Zennor` | a code block |
| holding a `<dl>` | `    - **Brisk**`, `        - Callow` | a code block |
| in a table cell | `\| - Elvar     - Fennick - Galt \|` | (one line, as every list in a cell) |

content.txt and chunks.jsonl write list lines as content.md does, and had the
same lines. The doctags are not affected: docling-core's doctags serializer
writes every nested list as a `<list_item>` of its own, after its parent's, so
a missing item and an empty one come out alike.

### P45-2: why not a marker line of its own

A Markdown list item with nothing on its marker's line is an empty item, and
CommonMark does not let a list that opens with one interrupt a paragraph. An
empty marker line works after a heading or a paragraph, but under an item with
text, `- Jaskov`, `    -`, `        - Kelmar` reads `-` as a setext underline:
`Jaskov` becomes an `<h2>` and the sub-list a code block. `- ` with a trailing
space reads the same.

CommonMark's own spelling of an item that holds a list is the list on the
item's line, `- - Gorvane`. Its content begins after the marker and up to four
spaces, so `-   - Gorvane`, the marker padded to four columns, puts the inner
list where docling indents nested lists, and the next line, `    - Holvish`,
is its sibling. It reads correctly in every shape above, numbered ones
included (`6.  - Varrick`), and in chains (`-   -   - Nalder`).

### P45-3: the fix

- **The backend makes the item.** Before the backend parses the page,
  `mark_empty_items` writes a third noncharacter, U+FDD2, as the text of each
  `<li>` of a `<ul>` or `<ol>` whose content outside its own lists is
  whitespace and empty wrappers (inline elements, `div`, `p`) and which holds a
  `<ul>`, `<ol>` or `<dl>`. Not a `<br>`: the backend writes one as its own
  character, U+E000, which counts as text, so it already makes an item of
  `<li><br><ul>…</ul></li>`; marked, that item's text was U+E000 beside the
  stand-in, which the stray check then caught. The backend then makes an item of it, counts
  it, and puts its lists inside it, so an `<ol start>` numbers the items after
  it right. As with P14-56's join markers, a marked page opens with a
  byte-order mark. The marked page is built in one pass: slicing it once per
  mark copies the page each time, and 2,000 items on a 1.1 MB page took 1.5 s
  that way. P14-56's join markers were inserted so too, and 2,000
  sub/superscripts on that page took 3.2 s; P48 builds them in one pass.
- **content.json holds the item empty.** Once the document is built the
  item's text and `orig` are emptied. content.json gains an empty `list_item`
  holding its list, numbered among its siblings, as the page has it. The
  doctags do not change.
- **Each text surface writes it on its list's first line.** While content.md,
  content.txt and the chunks are written, the empty item carries the stand-in
  again, so its line is `marker U+FDD2`, which nothing else can produce.
  `write_empty_items` joins that line to the next one, padding the marker to
  where the next line's list begins: `-   - Gorvane`, `2.  1. Raskel`,
  `    -   - Kelmar`. A marker too wide for four columns (`1000.`), or no deeper
  line after it, keeps a line of its own with the marker alone. In a table
  cell, where docling writes a list on one line, the item is its marker before
  its list's first: `- - Elvar`.
- **An empty item has no text to tell chrome by.** The bridge moves each text
  that is not header, nav, footer or aside text from the furniture layer to the
  body. An empty item now goes where its own items went; moved on its own, a
  nav menu's empty item was a bare `-` in content.md.
- **Absence is said, not hidden.** A page with U+FDD2 of its own, as the
  character or as a reference to it, is not marked and gets a warning.
  `html.unescape` drops a reference to a noncharacter, which the backend's
  parser decodes, so the check looks for the reference itself. A stand-in
  found anywhere but its item's line is removed and named in a warning, as
  P14-56 does for a join marker.

Only an item with no text of its own changes. Over 600 seeded random list
trees (up to five levels deep, either kind, `start` numbers, one or two lists in an
item, whitespace in the empty item, after a paragraph or under an item with
text), the 213 pages with no such item were byte-identical to master on every
surface, and in the 387 with one, every list read back with a CommonMark
reader as the page has it. The tree generator left out three shapes docling
writes wrongly with or without this change; they are in P45-5.

### P45-4: real files

Every document in the real-file folder P27, P28 and P40 scanned, copied first
and read only: 256 files (82 Word, 23 decks, 6 workbooks, 1 EPUB, 5
zips, 62 CSVs, 58 Markdown files, 19 HTML files). Each was rendered into its
page twice, with master's MarkItDown bridge and with P40's (#193), which keeps
the nesting master's flattened; an HTML file is its own page. Each page was
then extracted with master's docling bridge and this one, without a browser.

- **3 files render on neither**, on WebShot's own archive limits: a symbolic
  link in a zip, and a deck and a zip that expand past 100 MB.
- **94 pages hold no `<li>`** (93 of P40's), so nothing is marked and every
  step added here does nothing: 59 CSVs, 13 Word files, 10 decks, every
  workbook. They were not extracted twice; docling's DocTags export of a
  large table is quadratic, and one CSV took minutes.
- **154 pages hold lists but no such item** (136 of P40's): content.json,
  content.md, content.txt, the doctags, the chunks, the tables and the
  warnings are byte-identical to master's.
- **5 pages hold such items, all Word files: 36 items**, 24 of them holding
  a list of more than one item on P40's pages (15 on master's, which flatten
  some of the rest, P40-1). Read back with markdown-it-py, master's
  content.md holds none of the 36 with its list; this one holds all 36, on
  either page. content.md and content.txt each change on 25 lines, and every
  one is an item's line joined to its list's first: in one outline 11 lines
  hold two items, an empty item holding an empty item (`-   -   1. …`).
  content.json gains the 36 empty items, and its other texts are unchanged in
  text, marker and layer. The chunks change on the same lines and keep their
  count; the doctags, the tables and the warnings do not change. None of the
  36 is in a list with a start number, so no number changes.
- **Captured end to end** through Chromium with P40's tree and each docling
  bridge, the outline's content.md changes on exactly the scan's lines, its
  doctags, `assets.json` and `links.json` are identical, and the manifest's
  count of content.json items rises by the 24 empty items, 80 to 104.

Extraction of each changed page, best of five, stayed within 10 ms of
master's (the outline: 42 ms, now 52 ms). On a synthetic 231 KB page with 300
such items extraction took 3.2 s rather than 2.8 s, docling handling 300 more
items; with 600 ordinary nested lists instead, the two took the same. The
pass that finds the items is skipped on a page with no `<li`, and costs 0.24 s
on a 1.2 MB page with 2,000 of them.

### P45-5: what this does not cover

- **An item with no text of its own holding a list and something else** is
  left to docling as before. With an image or a table, docling drops the item
  and the image or table with it, from content.json and content.md, with no
  warning; the same happens to an image or a table that is all an item holds
  (P52 makes the item in both cases). With a checkbox it writes the checkbox as an item of
  its own, `- [ ]`, and the list after it; a code block is P50's, which reads
  it as a block of code under the item.
- **`<li></li>`**, an item with nothing in it, still has no line.
- **A `<br>` in an item** is the backend's U+E000 in the item's text, which
  reaches content.json, content.md and content.txt on master as it does here
  (found by the session extending this fix, and flagged separately).
- **A marker four characters wide or more** (`1000.`): the item keeps a bare
  marker line. docling's four-space indent does not nest a list under such a
  marker anyway, item text or not. (A picture or a table there goes one space
  past the marker, P61.)
- **docling's other list limits, unchanged:** a numbered list starting at
  other than 1 cannot interrupt a paragraph in CommonMark, so under an item
  with text it reads as that text; two lists of one kind in one item are
  written with nothing between them and read as one; and a nested list before
  the page's first heading is written flat, because the bridge moves its items
  to the body layer and leaves their groups behind (flagged separately).
- **P14-56's check for a page's own join markers** looks for the characters
  only, so a page writing U+FDD0 as `&#xFDD0;` loses it without a warning
  (flagged separately; this entry's check does not have the gap).

### P45-6: the tests

`tests/test_item_holding_a_list.py`, without a browser: the fixture's lists
read back from content.md with markdown-it-py as the page has them (against
master's bridge, 6 of its 7 sections do not); each shape's exact lines in
content.md, content.txt and the chunks; that an empty marker line would not do
(the `<h2>` and the code block); content.json's empty items, what they hold,
and `5.`, `6.`, `7.`; the nav menu staying chrome; the table cell; no stand-in
or byte-order mark in any surface and no warning; that against the unmarked
page only the items' nine lines change, each as expected; which items are
marked and which are left to docling (a `<br>` among them); a stand-in with no
line to share; a stray stand-in removed and named; and a page carrying U+FDD2,
as the character and three spellings of its reference.

## P35: MarkItDown guessed a text file's encoding from its first 64 KB (2026-10-11)

P33-3 recorded that a UTF-8 file whose first character outside ASCII comes
after its first 64 KB is decoded as ASCII and fails. MarkItDown 0.1.8 reads a
64 KiB sample (`_read_charset_sample`), asks charset-normalizer for its
encoding, and decodes the whole stream by that answer. Measured on P33's
branch at 34ae3b5, before P28, P29 and P33 merged, with MarkItDown 0.1.8,
Magika 0.6.2 and charset-normalizer 3.5.1 under Python 3.12 on macOS, with
the CI extras. The fixtures are `late_utf8.csv` and `late_utf8_archive.zip`
in `tests/fixtures/office/`, written by `tools/fixtures/office.py`.

### P35-1: which files failed

Each format was written with its first character outside ASCII at about
70 KB, on its own and as a zip member:

| Format | On its own | In a zip |
|---|---|---|
| CSV, TSV | exit 2: `UnicodeDecodeError` from MarkItDown's CSV reader | left out, named (P33) |
| JSON, JSON Lines, XML, `.txt` | exit 2: `UnicodeDecodeError` from its plain-text reader | left out, named |
| YAML | exit 2, as above, or "No converter attempted a conversion" | left out, named, or counted as a format WebShot has no reader for |
| Notebook, Python | not a format on its own | left out, named |
| `.ini`, `.sql`, `.sh` | not a format on its own | counted as a format WebShot has no reader for |

Whether a given file failed depends on Magika as much as on its format.
MarkItDown guesses an encoding only for a stream Magika names as text; where
Magika's name agrees with the suffix, its guess is the only one. A stream
Magika could not name, or named as something its suffix is not, went first to
a reader chosen by the suffix with no encoding, and MarkItDown's plain-text and
CSV readers then guess from all of the bytes, which works. So the CSV above
failed when its last row was `café,1` and read when it ended in a longer
sentinel Magika could not name; a `.txt` of `x` lines ending in `café` failed
where a `.log` of the same bytes read. YAML has no MIME type in Python 3.12's
`mimetypes`, so a YAML file Magika could not name was taken by no reader at
all: a late `é` did it, and so did a byte order mark in front of a one-line
file. A short text file behind a byte order mark that Magika did name was
read, and the mark put at the start of the page as U+FEFF.

The guess was not only wrong past the sample. A CSV that is not UTF-8 is
read by WebShot as UTF-8 before MarkItDown sees it (`_as_escaped_csv`), so its
accented letters became U+FFFD; charset-normalizer then took the UTF-8 that
WebShot wrote, U+FFFD's bytes and all, for Shift JIS 2004, and the page showed
`caf魹ｽ`. On a real zip it read a UTF-8 file of box-drawing characters, inside
the sample, as `ptcp154`, a Kazakh code page (P35-4). Neither said a word.

### P35-2: the encoding WebShot states

`_convert_bytes`, the one path for a file and a member (P29-2), now gives
MarkItDown an encoding wherever WebShot has one that is not a guess:

- **Bytes WebShot wrote** are UTF-8: the CSV `_as_escaped_csv` makes, from a
  CSV or a TSV.
- **Text that decodes as UTF-8 to its last byte**, with a character outside
  ASCII and no NUL, is declared UTF-8 (`_declared_charset`). A legacy
  encoding all but never forms valid UTF-8 sequences, and a NUL, which text
  does not hold, keeps a binary file that happens to from being read as text
  on WebShot's say-so. A byte order mark makes it `utf-8-sig`, which drops the
  mark: it records how the text is encoded and is not part of it.
  MarkItDown dropped it only where Magika could not name the file.

MarkItDown keeps a declared encoding in front of its own guess: where the two
disagree it tries the declared one first, and where Magika cannot name the
stream, the encoding is what lets its plain-text reader take it. Every case
in P35-1 that is UTF-8 now reads, on its own and in a zip, and the BOM never
reaches the page. A CSV or TSV that is not UTF-8 is still read as UTF-8, now
with a warning that says so: `The file is not UTF-8, the one encoding WebShot
reads a CSV or TSV file in, so the page shows U+FFFD (�) where its bytes are
not UTF-8`. A UTF-16 CSV, read as UTF-8 the same way, gets the same
warning.

Two things are left to MarkItDown's guess on purpose. ASCII, for which
charset-normalizer answered `ascii` or `utf-8`, both of which decode it as
itself; declaring it would only reorder MarkItDown's guesses, and so which
reader an unsuffixed member goes to. And text that is not UTF-8, whose
encoding WebShot has no better way to know (P35-3).

### P35-3: what this does not cover

Measured with the same matrix in Windows-1252, before and after; this change
leaves all of it as it was, except the CSV and TSV rows, which now warn:

- A late character still fails as P35-1 does, for every format Magika names
  as text.
- Where a reader guesses from all of the bytes, a few accented letters among
  80 KB of ASCII are too little for charset-normalizer. A `.txt` read as
  `cp1006` gave `cafﻠ` for `café`, and curly quotes as C1 control
  characters. Where it found no encoding at all, MarkItDown decoded the bytes
  as UTF-8 and dropped every one that was not: a `.py` lost its `é` and both
  curly quotes without a mark. Neither is in the manifest.
- An empty `.yaml`, `.yml` or `.xml` file on its own still ends the run with
  exit 2 and "No converter attempted a conversion", as before: no reader takes
  an empty stream Magika cannot name.

Choosing an encoding for legacy text, by charset-normalizer over all of the
bytes or by the Windows-1252 a browser assumes, and saying in the manifest
that it was chosen, is a decision of its own.

Apart from encodings: a table's capture costs time with the square of its
rows. docling-core's DocTags serializer reads `TableData.grid` once per row,
and each read builds the whole grid again, so a 1,000-row, 2-column CSV built
4 million cells in 2,010 reads, 23.6 s of a 76 s profiled capture. Captures of
500, 1,000 and 2,000 rows took 26 s, 57 s and 179 s (one run each, with other
test runs on the machine), and the first `late_utf8.csv`, 11,431 rows of
`x,1`, ran the round-trip test past 40 minutes. The fixtures reach 64 KB with
82 rows of long text instead; the cost itself is not changed here.

### P35-4: real files

Every `.zip`, `.csv`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.xml`, `.yaml`, `.log` and `.epub`
file in one real folder, 298 files, was read through `_render_local_file` by
P33's bridge and by this one; the dataset zip past the 100 MB limit, which
P33-1 read member by member, was read the same way: two CSVs, 707 MB between
them. Of the 300, 293 pages were byte-identical, one file failed on both, on
the archive guard's symbolic-link refusal, and six changed:

- **The zipped Python project.** Its vendored `pkg_resources/__init__.py`,
  first non-ASCII byte at 74,446 (P33-3), is in the page, 124,345 characters,
  and its warning is gone. Its vendored `rich/box.py`, UTF-8 box drawing from
  byte 370, had been guessed `ptcp154` and read as `в”Ңв”Җв”¬в”җ` where it says
  `┌─┬┐`; it now reads as the file does. No other member changed.
- **Five `.txt` files**, all saved with a byte order mark: each page had begun
  with an invisible U+FEFF, and no longer does. Nothing else in them changed.

Conversion took, P33's bridge then this one, one run each: 210.7 s and 206.3 s
for the CSVs (the dataset zip's two members among them), 6.6 s and 7.2 s for
the `.txt` files, 13.1 s and 13.0 s for the zips, and 5.3 s and 5.4 s for the
log, which is 41 MB.

### P35-5: the tests

`tests/test_text_charset.py` checks that every late character in the two
fixtures is past the 64 KiB sample, so a fixture regenerated shorter fails
rather than passing for nothing; that MarkItDown on its own, handed what the
bridge hands it less the encoding, still fails each late file and the marked
YAML and still puts the marked text's BOM on the page, which is the premise
of the rest; that the late CSV reads with no warning; that every member of
the archive is in the page, the Windows-1252 CSV with U+FFFD and the one
warning that names it; that neither marked member's BOM reaches the page; and
`_declared_charset` on ASCII, UTF-8, a BOM, Windows-1252, a NUL and nothing.
Against P33's bridge, its four tests of what reaches the page fail.
`tests/test_office_formats.py` captures both fixtures end to end and finds
their sentinels, each the late character's own words, in `content.md`,
`content.txt` and `chunks.jsonl`: 25 s for the CSV and 40 s for the archive,
whose five late members put about 400 KB of text on the page.

## P40: a list nested in a converted document's item was flattened (2026-10-11)

A Word item numbered `1.` with a bulleted sub-item and a numbered one came out
of mammoth as
`<ol><li>Alpha<ul><li>sub a</li></ul><ol><li>sub b</li></ol></li><li>Bravo</li></ol>`.
markdownify wrote `1. Alpha`, `   * sub a`, `   1. sub b`, `2. Bravo`, and the
page printed `* sub a` as text in Alpha's item, with `sub b` an item beside
Alpha. markdownify's `convert_li` indents every line of an item after its
first by the width of the item's marker: two spaces under `* `, three under
`1. `. Python-Markdown takes an indented list only at its `tab_length`, four.
Every converted document whose lists nest goes through that writer: a Word
file, an EPUB, an HTML file, and each of those inside a zip. P31-4 counted the
Word items it flattened. P32-5 left it for this entry, with two lists nested in
one item; the case in `test_adjacent_lists.py` that pinned such a pair as
upstream writes it is now `test_two_lists_in_one_item_stay_two`. Measured with MarkItDown 0.1.8, markdownify 1.2.3,
mammoth 1.11.0, Python-Markdown 3.10.3 (with `extra`, `sane_lists` and `toc`,
as `MARKDOWN_EXTENSIONS` renders), nh3 0.3.7 and docling-core 2.99.0, on master
f2be8dd. The fixtures are `nested_book.epub`, `nested_report.docx` and
`nested_archive.zip` in `tests/fixtures/office/`, written by
`tools/fixtures/office.py`. Every word in them is made up.

### P40-1: what each shape became

| In the document | markdownify's Markdown | On the page, before |
|---|---|---|
| bullets under bullets, numbers under numbers | the sub-list 2 or 3 spaces in | the sub-items became the parent list's own |
| bullets under numbers, numbers under bullets | the same | the sub-items printed into the parent's text: `Parent 1. Child one 2. Child two` |
| three levels, of either kind | 2 or 3 spaces a level | at best the third level nested in the second |
| under `10.` or a wider number | 4 spaces or more | nested, which is why P30-1's `<ol start="12">` fixture did |
| an item of two paragraphs | the second after a blank line, 2 or 3 spaces in | the second left the list and took the next item with it: `Two 2. Three` |
| two lists in one item | joined with no line between (P32-5) | the second list the first's text, or more of its items |
| text after a nested list | on the sub-list's last line: `+ subtail text` | the text run into the sub-item's last word |
| an item that holds only a list | the list on the marker's line: `* + x`, `  + y` | `y` an item of the outer list |
| a quotation in an item | `  > quoted` | a quotation in the item, as it should be |

Python-Markdown's rules, read from its `OListProcessor` and
`ListIndentProcessor` and measured on each shape: a line with a marker four to
seven spaces in begins a nested list, at any depth and under a marker of any
width. A line straight after a nested list is more of that list's last item,
whatever its indentation. A block after a blank line belongs to the item only
four spaces in, and the next item must then follow a blank line too, or it is
read as more of that block. A nested list with no blank line before it nests
only straight after the item's first block: after a later block it is that
block's text (`Two + sub`). On the item's first block, a `>` four spaces in is
text, not a quotation. A list begun on the marker's own line (`* + x`) reads a
list nested in `x` as `x`'s text. Under `sane_lists`, a bulleted list and a
numbered one with a blank line between are two lists, and two of one kind are
one, as P32 found.

### P40-2: four spaces, and a blank line after a nested list
